Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 1:

﴿Those who disbelieve and bar (others) from the way of Allah — He will render their deeds void.﴾

He introduced the exhortation to fighting with a preface explaining Allah's anger at the disbelievers, because of their disbelief, their barring of people from the religion of Allah, and their belittling of its matter before Allah. This is so that it would stir in the souls of the Muslims rage against them and aversion to them, so that the resolve to advance against the disbelievers would be aroused in them, and so that they would not be concerned with the strength they possess, when they know that Allah humiliates the polytheists and gives victory to the believers. This is thus a preparation for His saying: ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve...﴾ [Muhammad: 4].

(p. 73)
By beginning with the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") and its relative clause (al-silah, the clause that follows it), which contains the disbelief of those who disbelieved and their opposition to the religion of Allah, there is an arousing of curiosity for what follows of the ruling suited to the relative clause. There is also an indication, through the relative pronoun and its clause, of the cause of the ruling given in the predicate, namely: because of their disbelief and their barring. This is an excellent opening for the intended purpose.

Kufr (disbelief) here means associating partners with Allah, as is the Qur'anic usage wherever kufr is used without any indication that it refers to someone other than the polytheists.

This sentence includes three attributes of the polytheists: disbelief, barring from the way of Allah, and the squandering of deeds resulting from Allah's leaving them astray.

Barring from the way (al-sadd 'an al-sabil) is turning people away from following the religion of Islam, and turning themselves away from hearing the call of Islam, by an even stronger means.

The way (al-sabil) is attributed to Allah because it is the religion that Allah has chosen for His servants: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. The name "the way" is used metaphorically for the religion, because the religion leads to the pleasure of Allah, just as a road leads the traveller on it to his goal.

Among barring from the way of Allah is their barring of the Muslims from the Sacred Mosque. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they bar (others) from the way of Allah and the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Hajj: 25].

Among barring from the Sacred Mosque is their expulsion of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers from Makkah, and their barring of them from the 'umrah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah.

Among barring from the way of Allah is their feeding of people on the day of Badr, in order that they might remain steadfast alongside them and increase in number around them. For this reason it has been said that the verse was revealed concerning those who fed (the army) on the day of Badr, and they were twelve men from the chiefs of the polytheists of Quraysh. They are: Abu Jahl, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Nubayh ibn al-Hajjaj, Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj, Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham, al-Harith ibn Hisham, Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad, al-Harith ibn 'Amir ibn Nawfal, and Hakim ibn Hizam. This last one embraced Islam later and became one of the excellent Companions.

Also counted among them were Safwan ibn Umayyah, Suhayl ibn 'Amr, Muqays al-Jumahi, and al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and Abu Sufyan ibn Harb. These two embraced Islam and their Islam was good. Concerning the other three there is disagreement.

Among barring from the way of Allah is their barring of people from hearing the Qur'an: ﴿And those who disbelieve said: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you may overcome."﴾ [Fussilat: 26].

Al-idlal (leading astray, here: nullifying) means invalidating and wasting, and it goes back to al-dalal (going astray). Its origin is the error in the path that is taken to reach a place that is intended, and it implies the other meanings.

This term is especially fitting here, because Allah nullified their deeds which appear good, so He did not reward them for them, such as maintaining ties of kinship, feeding the hungry, and the like. Also, among the leading astray of their deeds is that most of their deeds were futile and evil. And among the leading astray of their deeds is that Allah frustrated their striving, so they gained nothing from it; they were defeated on the day of Badr, their feeding of the army went in vain, and their plotting and scheming against the Messenger (ﷺ) was corrupted, so they did not satisfy their rage on the day of Uhud. Then their defeats followed one another in all the battles. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to bar (others) from the way of Allah. They will spend it, then it will be for them a regret, then they will be overcome﴾ [al-Anfal: 36].

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds, and believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ), and it is the truth from their Lord, He will remove from them their misdeeds and set right their condition.﴾

This is the counterpart of the group of those who disbelieved, namely the group of those who believed and did righteous deeds. The mention of the relative pronoun and its clause indicates the reason for the statement and its cause, that is, because of their faith, He removed their misdeeds (﴿He removed from them their misdeeds﴾)...

The three attributes ascribed to the disbelievers are matched by three opposite attributes for the Muslims: faith, which is the opposite of disbelief; belief in what was sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ), which is the opposite of barring from the way of God; and doing righteous deeds, which is the opposite of part of what is contained in ﴿He rendered their deeds void﴾ (Muhammad 1). The phrase ﴿He removed from them their misdeeds﴾ is the opposite of another part of what is contained in ﴿He rendered their deeds void﴾ (Muhammad 1), and ﴿and set right their condition﴾ is the opposite of the remainder of what is contained in ﴿He rendered their deeds void﴾ (Muhammad 1).

On the side of the believers, the praise of the Qur'an is added through the parenthetical clause (al-jumla al-mu'tarida, a clause inserted between related parts of a sentence) ﴿and it is the truth from their Lord﴾.

This is parallel to its description as "the way of God" in His saying ﴿and who averted [others] from the way of God﴾ (Muhammad 1).

The Majesty (al-Jalala) is expressed here by the attribute of "Lord" in addition to honoring the Muslims, in the manner of His saying ﴿and that the disbelievers have no protector﴾ (Muhammad 11). Therefore He did not say: "and averted from the way of their Lord."

The expiation of misdeeds means their forgiveness. When they did righteous deeds, God expiated from them the misdeeds they had committed before faith, and expiated for them the minor sins, and expiated for them some of the major sins, in an amount known to Him, if they were few compared with their righteous deeds, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They mixed a righteous deed with another evil; perhaps God will turn to them in forgiveness﴾ (al-Tawba 102).

Al-bal (البال) is applied to the heart, that is, the intellect and the thoughts that occur to a person; this is its most common usage, and perhaps it is its literal meaning. Imru' al-Qays said:

*So he charged in a race between a bull and a she-goat, and the race of the wild beasts was on my mind.*

And he said:

*Over him is dust, evil in opinion and in mind.*

From it is their saying: "What is your bal?" meaning: "What did you think when you did such and such?" And their saying: "He does not care (la yubali)," as if it were derived from it, meaning: it does not occur to his mind. From it is the line of al-'Uqayli in al-Hamasa:

*We weep when we kill you, over you, and we kill you as if we did not care.*

That is, we do not think.

Al-Azhari transmitted from a group of scholars, regarding the meaning of "la ubali": "I do not dislike." End of quote.

I think they intended to explain the resulting meaning, and did not define the precise meaning of the word.

Al-bal is also applied to a state of affairs and a condition. In the hadith: "Every matter of importance (dhi bal) that does not begin with the praise of God is deficient (abtar)." The minister al-Batalyawsi said in his commentary on the Diwan of Imru' al-Qays: Abu Sa'id said: "I used to say to al-Ma'arri: 'How have you risen?' and he would say: 'In good, may God set right your bal.'" The author of al-Asas did not give it its due in explanation, and included it under the root (b-l-w).

Setting right the bal comprises setting right all affairs, because a person's conduct follows his opinion. So monotheism is the root of the believer's righteous condition, and from it arise the powers that resist the errors and delusions with which the people of polytheism were afflicted, which the Qur'an relates about them in many passages. The meaning is: He set straight their outlook and their intellects, so they think only what is good and reflect only on what succeeds.

﴿That is because those who disbelieve follow falsehood, and those who believe follow the truth from their Lord﴾

This explains the fundamental cause of the nullifying of the deeds of the disbelievers and the setting right of the state of the believers.

The use of the demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara) serves to distinguish the thing indicated in the most complete way, as an honouring of it. This demonstrative has been mentioned four times in these consecutive verses, for the purpose we have mentioned.

The demonstrative refers to the two preceding statements, namely ﴿He has sent their deeds astray﴾ [Muhammad: 1] and ﴿He removed from them their misdeeds and set right their affairs﴾ [Muhammad: 2], taking into account the two causes of these statements, which are derived from the two relative nouns (ism al-mawsul), the two relative clauses (silah), and what is conjoined to both of them.

The demonstrative noun is the subject (mubtada'), and his statement ﴿that those who disbelieve follow falsehood﴾, etc., is its predicate (khabar). The letter ba' is causal (lil-sababiyya), and what it governs is in the position of the predicate concerning the demonstrative noun. That is: this occurs because of the disbelievers following falsehood and the believers following the truth. Since this comprised both of the preceding statements, the predicate concerning it is connected to the two statements and is their cause.

In this there is the embellishment of combining after separating (muhassin al-jam' ba'd al-tafriq), which they call, like its reverse, al-tafsir (a figure of speech), because in combining there is an explanation (tafsir) of the meaning in which separate things share, whether they came earlier or later. Its evidence is the words of Hassan, from the style of this verse:

*A people who, when they make war, harm their enemy,*
*and when they seek to benefit their adherents, they benefit them.*

*That is a disposition in them, not newly arisen;*
*know that the worst of dispositions are innovations.*

Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: "This speech is called by the scholars of rhetoric al-tafsir." He means that it is one of the rhetorical embellishments (muhassinat badi'iyya). It is reported from al-Zamakhshari that he recited for himself, when he explained this verse to his students, and what he wrote in the margins was restricted from him, his statement:

*By it the horsemen were stricken, above their horses,*
*as the unmarried women were stricken beneath the curtains.*

*The swords slipped from their hands in bewilderment,*
*and the necklaces were shaken from their necks.*

[p. 77]

In this verse there is the embellishment of antithesis (tibaq) twice: between "those who disbelieved" and "those who believed," and between "the truth" and "falsehood." In the two verses of al-Zamakhshari there is the embellishment of antithesis once: between "above" and "beneath."

Following falsehood and following truth are two figurative representations (tamthiliyyan) for the two states of action: acting in accordance with what the leaders of shirk order their followers, and what the Qur'an calls to. That is: they acted by falsehood, and the others acted by truth.

Describing the truth as "from their Lord" is a means of honouring it and an ennobling of them.

* * *

﴿Thus does God strike examples for the people﴾

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to what precedes it. That is: just as that clarification of the two states, God clarifies the conditions for the people with a clear clarification.

The meaning: We have already made clear to each group of the disbelievers and the believers their state, in detail and in summary, and what it leads to in terms of deserving treatment, such that no obscurity remains regarding the reality of the two states. And with a clarification like that, God presents examples to the people, lest causes and effects become confused for them.

The meaning of "yadribu" (strikes) is "casts" (yulqi). This is a casting of clarification, by the context. It has been discussed earlier, at His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿that He should strike any example﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-amthal (examples) is the plural of mathal (with a vowel on the first letter), which is the state that represents its bearer, that is, makes him famous to the people and makes him known, so that he is not confused with his counterparts.

The lam is for purpose (lil-ajal), and by "the people" is meant all people. The pronoun in "their examples" refers to the people.

The meaning: Just as this clarification, God makes their states clear to the people, so that they do not remain heedless of the affairs of their own selves, hidden from realizing the reality of themselves by the veil of habituation, lest the bad become mixed with the good, and so that they may be possessed of insight in their affairs. In this there is an indication of the necessity of discernment (tawassum) to distinguish the hypocrites from those who are truly Muslims, for among the aims of the surah is warning against the hypocrites.

[78]

Without doubt, this verse was revealed after the Battle of Badr, because it contains His words, ﴿until, when you have subdued them, then bind their bonds﴾. This is the ruling that was revealed concerning the punishment for what happened at Badr regarding the ransoming of prisoners, referred to in His words, Exalted is He, (﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he inflicts a massacre upon the land﴾ [al-Anfal: 67]) and so on, since the ruling on that was not yet settled on that day. This was discussed in Surat al-Anfal.

The fa' (so) here links this statement to what precedes it: stirring up the hearts of the Muslims by denouncing the condition of the polytheists, showing the failure of their deeds, and honouring the condition of the Muslims and the soundness of their opinions.

The purpose is to diminish the standing of the enemy in the hearts of the Muslims and to urge them to cut off their root, so that the religion may be wholly for God, because that is greater than the benefit of ransoming their captives with money, so that the Muslims may worship their Lord in security. This refers to the verse in Surat al-Anfal and to what the ta'lil (causal clause) implies in His words, ﴿until the war lays down its burdens﴾.

(Idha) is a temporal adverb for the future, carrying the sense of a conditional, and this is its most common usage. The response of the condition is His words, ﴿then strike the necks﴾.

The "meeting" in His words, ﴿when you meet those who disbelieved﴾, means confrontation. This is a well-known usage of "liqa'" (meeting). One says, "the day of the liqa'," and by it nothing is understood except the meeting in battle. One also says, "If you meet so-and-so, you meet a lion from him." An-Nabigha said:

*Avoid the Banu Hunn, for meeting them is hateful,*
*even if you meet with nothing but their advance forces.*

So the meaning is not: "when you meet the disbelievers on the road or the like." Thus there is no need to mention a specifier for the verb "you meet."

The meaning is: when you fight the polytheists in the future, then persist in killing them until, when you see that you have broken their strength, you take captives from among them.

"Striking the necks" is a well-known kinayah (metonymy) by which killing is expressed, whether by striking, or by piercing the hearts with spears, or by shooting with arrows. It was preferred over the word "killing" because the use of the metonymy carries eloquence, and because this particular expression has a harshness and severity that suit the context of incitement.

Here "striking" means cutting with the sword, which is one of the modes of fighting among them, because it best demonstrates the bravery of the warrior, as he faces his enemy face to face.

The meaning is: kill them, whether the killing is by sword-striking, spear-thrusting, or arrow-shooting, because the purpose of all of this is subduing them (al-ithkhan).

"Those who disbelieved" means the polytheists, because the Qur'anic usage of the derivatives of the root k-f-r, such as "the disbelievers," "the unbelievers," and "those who disbelieved," is shirk (associating partners with God).

(Hatta) here is inceptive, and the sense of the limit carried with it ultimately amounts to the sense of a consequence.

Al-ithkhan means domination, because it leaves the defeated one like a thing that is "muthkhan," that is, heavy and firm, which does not move lightly. It is also used of a liquid that has congealed or nearly congealed, so that it does not flow easily. It is also used of a garment or a rope when its strands are many, so that they are hard to unravel.

Its use has become predominant for weakening the enemy by killing, and both meanings are present in this verse. If it is interpreted as domination, the meaning is: until, when you have overcome among them those who fall into your grip as captives, then bind their bonds. In that case, the permissibility of release (mann) and ransom (fida') is not restricted.

If al-ithkhan is interpreted as the great number of killings among them, the meaning is: until, when only a few of the army remain, then take them captive at that time, that is, spare the captives. Both possibilities involve some interpretive effort in the structure of the verse, but the first possibility is more evident. Its explanation has been given in Surat al-Anfal in His words, ﴿until he inflicts a massacre upon the land﴾ [al-Anfal: 67].

"Striking the necks" is in the accusative of the absolute object, being a substitute for its verb, then it was made into an annexation to its object. The implied sense is: "then strike the necks, striking." When the verb was omitted for brevity, the absolute object was placed before the direct object, and it took the place of the verb in governing that object, and it was annexed to the object, as nouns are annexed to nouns, because the verbal noun is predominantly nominal.

[80]

Al-shadd means the strength of binding and the strength of holding.

Al-wathaq, with a fatha on the waw, is the thing by which one is bound. It is permissible to pronounce the waw with a kasra, but this reading is not transmitted. Here it is a kinayah for captivity, because captivity entails being placed in a fetter with which the captive is bound.

The meaning is: kill them, and if you subdue some of them, take them captive.

The definiteness of "the necks" and "the bond" may be the mental (dhihni) definiteness, or it may be a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning: "then strike their necks, and bind their bonds."

Al-mann means bestowal. What is meant by it is releasing the captive and enslaving him not killing him, for enslavement is a favour upon him when he is not killed. Al-fida', with a kasra on the fa' and an extended vowel, is the release of the captive from captivity in exchange for a payment of money, or an exchange for Muslim captives in the hands of the enemy. He placed mann before fida' to give it preference, because it is more conducive to gaining the heart of the one who is shown favour, so that he may be made to serve the favour-giver with part of himself.

"Mann" and "fida'" are in the accusative as absolute objects, substituting for their governing verbs. The implied sense is: "either you bestow favour, or you ransom."

His words "after" (ba'du) mean: after the subduing. This is a restriction on the permissibility of release and ransom. That is left to the judgment of the commander of the army according to what he sees as the interest in one of the two options, as the Prophet (ﷺ) did after the battle of Hawazin. This is the apparent meaning of the verse, and the default is that it is not abrogated. This is the view of the majority of the jurists and scholars of reasoning.

Therefore His words, "those who disbelieved," are general, covering every disbeliever, that is, every polytheist. It includes the men who are known for fighting, and it includes those who fought alongside them from among the women, children, monks, and rabbis. This verse serves to define the states of fighting and what follows it, not to specify the time of fighting, nor to identify who the disbelievers are, because the times of fighting are specified in Surat Bara'a (al-Tawba). The identity of the disbelievers is known from the Qur'anic usage in His words, ﴿So when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5].

Then it appears that this verse was revealed after the verse in Surat al-Anfal, ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he inflicts a massacre upon the land﴾ [al-Anfal: 67]. The scholars differed concerning the ruling of this verse regarding killing, release, and ransom. The view adopted by Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Thawri, and al-Awza'i,

[81]

and one of two reported positions from Abu Hanifa, transmitted by al-Tahawi, and among the early generation 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, 'Ata', and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, is that this verse is not abrogated, and that it requires a choice regarding the captive polytheists between killing, release, or ransom, with the commander of the army having discretion in that matter. It seems that the proponents of this view hold that the subject of the verse is the permission of release or ransom, so it is either abrogating or terminating the ruling of His words, Exalted is He, (﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he inflicts a massacre upon the land﴾ [al-Anfal: 67]) up to His words, ﴿a great punishment would have touched you for what you took﴾ [al-Anfal: 68], in Surat al-Anfal.

This is preferable to making it abrogating His words, Exalted is He, ﴿kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5], because, as you know, the subject of that verse is specifying the times of truce and the times of war. Therefore those scholars did not hold a prohibition on killing a captive, whereas the choice here is between release and ransom, and killing is not mentioned alongside them. It is firmly established in the Sahih, through widespread transmission, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) killed al-Nadr ibn al-Harith from among the captives of Badr, and this was before the revelation of this verse, and 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt. He also killed the captives of Qurayza who had submitted to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, and he killed Hilal ibn Khatal and Miqyas ibn Subaba on the day of the conquest of Makkah, and after Uhud he killed Abu 'Izza al-Jumahi the poet. All of this does not contradict this verse, because it has given the choice to the one in authority.

Also, the permissibility of enslavement is not mentioned in this verse, though it is the original ruling concerning captives. It is included in release if release is understood to encompass the abandonment of killing. Moreover, the pairing of release with ransom implies that enslavement is legislated. It was narrated by Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb from Malik that release is a form of manumission.

Al-Hasan and 'Ata' said: the choice is between release and ransom only, without killing the captive, so killing a captive is forbidden. The apparent meaning of this verse supports the view of al-Hasan and 'Ata'.

A group of scholars held that this verse is abrogated, and that it is not permissible concerning a captive polytheist except killing, by His words, Exalted is He, ﴿kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5]. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and Ibn Jurayj, and it was transmitted by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the well-known position of Abu Hanifa. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, two of Abu Hanifa's companions, said: there is no harm in ransoming captive polytheists who have not embraced Islam in exchange for captive Muslims held by the polytheists. Al-Jassas reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) ransomed two Muslim captives in exchange for a polytheist captive from Thaqif.

The limit derived from "until" in His words, ﴿until the war lays down its burdens﴾, is for causation not for restriction. That is, for the sake of the war laying down its burdens, meaning so that the polytheists may refrain from war, and you may be secure from war waged against you. It is not a limit on the ruling of fighting.

The meaning is that this ruling continues in this manner so that the enemy may be weakened and thus abandon fighting you. Therefore this limit has no implied meaning (mafhum) of its own. The causal clause is connected to His words, ﴿then strike the necks﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion. The implied sense is: "strike the necks," that is, do not abandon killing for the sake of the war laying down its burdens. It is therefore given as instruction and admonition, meaning: do not occupy yourselves at the encounter either with killing those who disbelieved, in order that the war may lay down its burdens. Then, when you have overcome them, occupy yourselves with sparing those whom you overpower by capture, so that release or ransom may follow afterward.

Al-awzar means burdens. The laying down of burdens is a metaphor for the completion of the task. The state of the end of fighting is likened to the state of a porter or a traveler setting down his loads. This is one of the novel expressions of the Qur'an. 'Abd Rabbih al-Sulami, or Sulaym al-Hanafi, took from it his saying:

*So she cast down her staff, and the journey's end settled her,*
*as the traveler's eye is comforted by returning home.*

He likened the state of one who has ended a hardship to the state of a traveler who casts down the staff he carried during his journey.

[83]

His words, ﴿That, and had God willed, He would have avenged Himself upon them, but that He might test some of you by means of others﴾: the demonstrative was repeated after His words just before, ﴿That is because those who disbelieved followed falsehood﴾ [Muhammad: 3], for the subtle purpose mentioned there. It is the predicate of an omitted subject, or a subject whose predicate is omitted. The omitted part is: "the matter is that," and what is pointed to is what preceded, from His words, ﴿then strike the necks﴾ up to here. The demonstrative conveys the affirmation of the ruling and its firm establishment in souls.

The clause consisting of the demonstrative and the omitted element is a parenthetical insertion. His words, ﴿had God willed, He would have avenged Himself upon them﴾, are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the implied pronoun in the verbal noun in His words, ﴿then strike the necks﴾.

That is: you were commanded to strike their necks, while God, had He willed, would have destroyed them and not imposed fighting on you. But God attached effects to their ordinary causes, and these are that He tests some of you by means of others.

The verb "avenged" (intasara) is followed by the preposition "min" although its proper complement would be "ʿala," because it is used with the meaning of "retaliated" (intaqama).

The contrast (istidrak) refers back to what is implicit in the sense of the will, namely the possibility that God left retaliation against them for a reason other than what follows the contrast.

Al-balw in its basic sense means testing and trial, and here it is used figuratively for its consequence, which is the manifestation of what God intended: the elevation of the ranks of the believers, the infliction of the dread of them upon the hearts of their enemies, and the humiliation of the disbelievers, whose condition becomes visible to people's sight and hearing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 4–6 (part 2 of 2):

(﴿And those who fight in the way of Allah — He will never waste their deeds﴾ ﴿He will guide them and set right their affairs﴾ ﴿and admit them to Paradise, which He has made known to them﴾)

This is among the manifestations of the trial of some of them by means of others, and it is the counterpart of what is in His saying ﴿so strike the necks﴾ up to His saying ﴿and then either release them as a favour or [accept] ransom﴾. For that is among the manifestations of the humiliation of those who disbelieve, so there is mentioned here what is among the elevation of those of the believers who fought in the way of Allah, by Allah's care for them.

The clause (﴿And those who were killed in the way of Allah﴾) etc. is a conjunction with the clause ﴿so when you meet those who disbelieve, then strike the necks﴾ etc., for when He commanded them to fight the polytheists, He followed the command with the promise of reward for doing it.

The mention of "those who fought in the way of Allah" is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun, whereas the expected form by the apparent structure would have been: "He will never waste Allah's deeds of yours," and so on in the address style. So the apparent form of pronoun was departed from to the explicit noun, so that the fronting of the predicate-bearing subject before the verbal predicate would give a benefit that strengthens the predicate, and so that it would serve as a means to the use of the relative pronoun, to highlight its relative clause, and to indicate that the reason the predicate is built upon the relative clause is that this relative clause is the cause of what follows it of the predicate.

Page 84

So the clause ﴿so He will never waste their deeds﴾ is the predicate of the relative pronoun, and it is joined with the particle "fa" to convey causality, in that what follows the "fa" is consequent upon the relative clause of the relative pronoun, because the relative pronoun often carries the meaning of a conditional, so its predicate is joined with "fa." By this, the past form of the verb in (qatalu, "they fought") is directed to the future, because that is what the conditional requires.

His words, ﴿That, and had God willed, He would have avenged Himself upon them, but that He might test some of you by means of others﴾: the demonstrative was repeated after His words just before, ﴿That is because those who disbelieved followed falsehood﴾ [Muhammad: 3], for the subtle purpose mentioned there. The clause (﴿And those who were killed in the way of Allah﴾) etc. is a conjunction with the clause ﴿so when you meet those who disbelieve, then strike the necks﴾ etc., for when He commanded them to fight the polytheists, He followed the command with the promise of reward for doing it.

The mention of "those who fought in the way of Allah" is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun, whereas the expected form by the apparent structure would have been: "He will never waste Allah's deeds of yours," and so on in the address style. So the apparent form of pronoun was departed from to the explicit noun, so that the fronting of the predicate-bearing subject before the verbal predicate would give a benefit that strengthens the predicate, and so that it would serve as a means to the use of the relative pronoun, to highlight its relative clause, and to indicate that the reason the predicate is built upon the relative clause is that this relative clause is the cause of what follows it of the predicate.

So the clause ﴿so He will never waste their deeds﴾ is the predicate of the relative pronoun, and it is joined with the particle "fa" to convey causality, in that what follows the "fa" is consequent upon the relative clause of the relative pronoun, because the relative pronoun often carries the meaning of a conditional, so its predicate is joined with "fa." By this, the past form of the verb in (qatalu, "they fought") is directed to the future, because that is what the conditional requires.

The clause ﴿He will guide them﴾ and what is conjoined to it is an explanation of the clause ﴿He will never waste their deeds﴾.

The discussion has already preceded concerning the meaning of the wasting of deeds and the setting right of affairs.

Or the meaning is that He guided them to its path in the Hereafter, so they do not hesitate that they will enter it, and this is part of hastening the joy in it. It has been said that "'arrafaha" means He placed in it a fragrance ('arf), i.e., a pleasant scent, and perfuming is part of the completeness of good hospitality.

The majority read "qatalu" with the form of mufa'ala (qatalu, "they fought"), so it is a promise to the fighters, both living and dead. So the sentence is a fresh resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) for this occasion. The encouragement opens with addressing them by the attribute of faith, both to give weight to the speech and to indicate that faith requires this of them. The meaning of their supporting Allah is supporting His religion and His Messenger (ﷺ), because Allah is free of need for support in carrying out His will, as He said: ﴿And had Allah willed, He would have taken vengeance upon them﴾ [Muhammad: 4].

There is no need to posit an omitted noun between "tansuru" (you support) and the Name of Allah, such as "the religion of Allah," because one says "so-and-so supported so-and-so" when he supports his kin even though he is not present.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 8–9:

And al-ta's (ta's): misery (al-shaqa'), and it is applied to several meanings: destruction (al-halak), frustration (al-khayba), abasement (al-inhitat), and falling (al-suqut), and these are meanings that revolve around misery. It is very common to say: "ta'san lahu" (ruin to him), to the one who stumbles and is hated, meaning a fall and a prostration from which there is no rising. Its counterpart is their saying to the one who stumbles: "la'an lahu" (elevation to him), meaning rising up. Al-A'sha said:

With a she-camel of a fine, swift build, whenever she stumbles, ta's is more fitting for her than my saying "la'a."

And in the hadith of the slander (hadith al-ifk): "Umm Mistah stumbled in her cloak and said: 'Ta'isa Mistah' (may Mistah be ruined), because stumbling is ta's."

Among the marvels of the Qur'an is the occurrence of ﴿fa-ta'san lahum﴾ regarding the disbelievers in contrast to His saying to the believers: ﴿and He will make your feet firm﴾ [Muhammad: 7].

Page 86

The verb from ta's comes in the pattern of (manaʿa) and the pattern of (samiʿa). In the Qamus: when you address someone, you say "ta'asta" like "manaʿa," and when you report, you say "ta'isa" like "samiʿa."

Ta'san is in the accusative as an absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq) replacing its verb. The estimated sense is: "fa-ta'isu ta'sahum" (so may they be ruined with their ruin), and it is of the type of the idafa of the verbal noun to its agent, like "tabban lahu" and "waykhan lahu." The purpose of the idafa is to restrict ta's to them; then the lam of specification (lam al-tabyin) was introduced upon the agent, so it became ta'san lahum. The prepositional phrase is related to the verbal noun, or to its deleted governing verb according to the verified view, and this is the preference of Ibn Malik and his father Ibn Hisham.

It is also possible that ta'san lahum is used as a supplication against them, for the purpose of belittling and denouncing them, and this is among the usages of this construction, like "saqyan lahu," "ra'yan lahu," "tabban lahu," and "waykhan lahu." In that case, the verse necessarily contains a deleted verb of saying, whose estimate is: "fa-qala Allahu: ta'san lahum," or "fa-yuqalu: ta'san lahum."

The fa' entered upon ta'san, which is the predicate of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), to treat the relative pronoun as a conditional (al-shart).

His saying ﴿and He made their deeds go astray﴾ is a reference to what preceded at the beginning of the surah in His saying ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah – He will make their deeds go astray﴾ [Muhammad: 1]. The discussion on ﴿He made their deeds go astray﴾ [Muhammad: 1] has already occurred there.

The discussion of His saying ﴿That is because they hated﴾ and so on concerns its meaning, its position within the sentence before it, and the wisdom of its repetition, as previously mentioned in His saying ﴿That is because those who disbelieved followed falsehood﴾ [Muhammad: 3].

The reference is to the ta's and the misguiding of deeds mentioned earlier. Al-karahiyya: hatred and enmity.

And ﴿what Allah revealed﴾ is the Qur'an and what it contains of monotheism, prophethood, and resurrection. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Grievous to the polytheists is what you call them to﴾ [al-Shura: 13].

The ba' in ﴿because they hated﴾ is causal (lil-sababiyya).

Ihbat al-a'mal is their nullification: that is, making them void, i.e., wasted, with no benefit to them from them. What is meant by "their deeds" are the deeds from which they hoped for benefit in this world, since they did not hope for their benefit in the Hereafter, as they did not believe in resurrection. Rather, they hoped from righteous deeds for the pleasure of Allah and the pleasure of the idols, so that they might live in abundant provision, safety, and well-being, and that their children and livestock would be preserved. So it is more specific than the misguiding of their deeds, as you have learned at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah – He made their deeds go astray﴾ [Muhammad: 1] at the beginning of the surah.

The purpose of mentioning this specific after the general is to alert that they did not benefit from them, lest the believers think that they might lighten the punishment for them, for they used to ask about this, as in the hadith of "Adi ibn Hatim, that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about deeds that he used to practice in the Jahiliyya, such as manumission and the like. From the mention of this specific after the general, there has resulted an emphasis on the good mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 10:

﴿Have they not traveled through the earth and observed what was the end of those before them? God destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are the like of it.﴾ This is a consequence drawn from the statement ﴿But those who disbelieve, for them is destruction﴾ [Muhammad: 8], and the discussion of its counterparts, ﴿Have they not traveled through the earth﴾ [Ghafir: 82], has already been presented in Surat al-Rum and in Surat Ghafir.

The interrogation here is confirmatory (taqriri), and the meaning is: Is not the ruin of those who disbelieve evident, witnessed in its traces, through the evil end of their likes who lived before them and who followed a religion like theirs?

The clause ﴿God destroyed them﴾ is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), and this is an allusive threat (ta'ridh bi'l-tahdid). Al-tadmir (destruction) means annihilation and ruin, and it is the perishing itself.

The verb dammara is transitive to the one destroyed directly, so one says dammarahumu Allah (God destroyed them). In the verse, it is made transitive by the preposition of elevation (ist'la') for the sake of emphasizing the intensity of the destruction. The object of dammara is therefore omitted to intend generality, and then the destruction is made to fall upon them, which conveys the meaning of "dammara" covering everything that pertains to them. The omitted object is what is meant, and the fact that the destruction falls upon them means they are included within its scope.

The clause ﴿and for the disbelievers there are the like of it﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh) between the clause ﴿Have they not traveled through the earth﴾ and the clause ﴿That is because God is the protector of those who believe﴾ [Muhammad: 11]. By "the disbelievers" is meant the disbelievers of Mecca, and the meaning is: for your disbelievers there are the likes of the end of those before them, of destruction. This is an explicit statement of what was alluded to, for the sake of emphasis through generalization and then particularization.

Amthal (likes) is the plural of mithl, with a kasra on the mim and a sukun on the tha'. The plural is used because God uprooted the disbelievers several times until Islam was firmly established: He uprooted their chieftains on the day of Badr by the sword, on the day of Hunayn also by the sword, He sent the wind against them on the day of the Trench (al-Khandaq) and it routed them, and He cast terror and humiliation upon them on the day of the conquest of Mecca. All of this is similar to what He sent upon the nations in its purpose, which is the victory of the Messenger ﷺ and his religion. God has made what He gave His Messenger ﷺ of greater value by its being wrought by His hand and the hands of the believers directly with their swords, and that is more painful to the enemy.

The pronoun in "amthaluha" (its likes) refers to ʿāqibat (the end) of those before them, considering that it is a state of evil.

﴿That is because Allah is the Protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector.﴾ The demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara, "demonstrative") is repeated to refer back to the same reason stated earlier in His words ﴿That is because those who disbelieve follow falsehood﴾ [Muhammad: 3] and His words ﴿That is so; and had Allah willed, He would have taken vengeance upon them﴾ [Muhammad: 4].

The demonstrative refers to the content of His words ﴿and for the disbelievers there are its like﴾ [Muhammad: 10], in the sense of "that which has been mentioned," because it contains a threat to the polytheists of destruction. In their destruction there is a victory for the believers over the harm they suffered from them. Thus it is conveyed that what Allah threatened them with is caused by the fact that Allah is the helper of those who believe. This is the purpose of the causal clause, and what follows it is a completion.

[p. 89]

Here al-mawla means the ally and the helper. The meaning is that Allah helps those who help His religion, and they are those who believe, and He does not help those who disbelieve in Him and associate others with Him in His divinity. If He does not help them, then they find no helper, because no one can help them against Allah. Thus the category of "protector" is negated for them in this sense of al-mawla.

His words ﴿and the disbelievers have no protector﴾ convey two things: that Allah does not help them, and that when He does not help them, they have no helper. As for the affirmation of a protector for the polytheists in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Then We will say to those who associated [others with Allah], "Stay in your place, you and your partners"﴾ [Jonah: 28] up to His words ﴿and they will be returned to Allah, their true Master﴾ [Jonah: 30], that protector has another meaning, which is the owner and the lord.
