Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 13:

﴿And how many a town, mightier in strength than your town which has expelled you, have We destroyed, so there was no helper for them.﴾

This is a continuation (ʿatf) upon the clause "Have they not travelled in the land" (afalam yasirū fi al-ard), and what lies between them is an digression (istitrad) whose parts are connected to one another.

The word (ka'ayyin) indicates a large number, and it has been discussed in the commentary on Surat Al ʿImran and in Surat al-Hajj.

The intended meaning of "town" (qarya) is its people, by the indication of His saying "We destroyed them." The report was directed at the town and its pronoun in order to convey the comprehensiveness of all its people and all their conditions, and so that the attribution of the expulsion of the Messenger to the whole town carries the responsibility upon all its people, whether those who took charge of the causes of the expulsion or those who looked on and did not forbid it. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they expelled you from your homes and backed one another in your expulsion﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 9].

This is an amplification (itnab) in the threat, because the situation of threat and rebuke calls for amplification. The implication of this verse therefore reinforces the implication of His saying: ﴿So let them travel through the earth and see what was the end of those before them. Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers is the like thereof﴾ [Muhammad: 10]. Thus the confirmation of that was achieved through what is close to it, namely the destruction of nations possessing towns and cities, after His saying "those before them" had included whoever was among the people of towns. Here it adds the explicit statement that those before them were mightier in strength than they, so that they would understand that the destruction of these is easy for Allah. For when the preceding threat was a threat of the punishment of the sword, from His saying: ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, strike the necks﴾ [Muhammad: 4] and the verses that follow, it might cast into their souls a delusion, that their extermination by the sword is unattainable, given their strength and that their town, Mecca, and its sanctity among the Arabs protect them, so that the Arabs would not hold back from supporting them. Thus they might make light of this warning and not be humbled by this threat. So Allah informed them that many towns had been mightier in strength than their town, yet Allah destroyed them, and they found no helper.

By this the striking placement of the consequence (tafri') in His saying "so there was no helper for them" becomes apparent. He also added the idafa in His saying "your town," and described it as "which has expelled you," because of what the attribution of the town to the pronoun of the Messenger ﷺ conveys of blaming its people with the disgrace of severing ties, and because of what the relative clause indicates of the causal reason for their destruction, namely their expelling the Messenger ﷺ from his town. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And expel them from where they expelled you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191].

The application of the word "expulsion" (ikhraj) to the treatment the polytheists meted out to the Prophet ﷺ of harshness, harm, and resistance to the spread of the religion is an application by way of metaphor (istiʿara), because their evil treatment of him was the cause of his leaving Mecca, which was his town. So the cause of the departure was likened to the act of expulsion, and then the verb "expelled you" (akhrajatka) was applied to it. This is not truly an expulsion but a departure, for the polytheists did not compel the Prophet ﷺ to leave by expulsion; rather, on the contrary, they watched to prevent him from departing, fearing that he would take refuge with tribes that would support him. Therefore he concealed the matter of his migration from the people, except from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. So his saying "expelled you" is of the type of your saying: "He made me come to his land; it is my right over so-and-so," and it is a metaphor in the strict sense, not a rational metaphor (majaz ʿaqli), since there is no actual expulsion to which one could claim that its cause is in the position of the agent of expulsion. Nor is it a metonymy (kinaya), although Shaykh ['Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani] exemplified the rational metaphor with it in Dala'il al-I'jaz; an example suffices with supposition and possibility.

From the report of Allah's destroying them is derived the report of the negation of any kind of helper for them, that is, a rescuer who would save them from destruction.

The purpose is to remind that such polytheists as these found no repeller to ward off destruction from them. This is an allusion to despairing the polytheists of finding a helper who would support them in their war against the Muslims, cutting off whatever might stir in the souls of the polytheists that they could not be defeated because the tribes of the Arabs would back them. For this reason they formed the confederates (al-ahzab) at the Battle of the Trench.

The pronoun in "them" (hum) refers back to "town" (min qarya), because what is meant by the towns is their people. The meaning is:

We destroyed them with a destruction that left none of them surviving, for the survival of any of them would be a helper to that survivor by his deliverance from destruction.

The noun of agency in His saying "so there was no helper" (fa-la nasir) is intended as a generic noun, since it follows the negating "la" of genus. Therefore it is not intended to include any specific time, because it is not meant in the sense of a verb; rather, it is the mere attribution of the verbal noun, so it is purely nominal, and there is no regard to any of the three tenses. Accordingly, the meaning of "so there was no helper for them" is: no one helped them in the past. There is no need to treat what occurred in the past as if it were the present; the saying of the grammarians that the noun of agency is literally for the present follows the usual case when it is meant in the sense of the verb.

The reading of the majority is "wa-ka'ayyin" with a hamza after the kaf and the yaa shaddada. Ibn Kathir read it with an alif after the kaf and the yaa lightened, with kasra, and this is a dialectal form.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 14:

﴿Is one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord like one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive, while they follow their desires?﴾

This is a consequential clause (tafri') following the statement ﴿We destroyed them, and they had no helper﴾ [Muhammad: 13], to confirm that they have no helper. The confirmation returns to the allusive (ta'ridi) meaning in the speech, so it resembles an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani, a sentence that answers an implied question) but is expressed in the form of a consequential clause.

It is also possible that it is a consequential clause following what came before, His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ [Muhammad: 12] and so on. In that case it has the status of a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD), because it is a consequence of a parenthetical insertion.

This is a variation (tafannun) in the styling of speech, to renew the attention of the listeners, and it is among the styles that the Qur'an originated in Arabic speech.

The interrogative is used to deny the equivalence that the particle of comparison (ka-, "like") requires.

The purpose of denying the resemblance between these and those is to give preference to the first group, and to deny the claim of the polytheists that they are better than the believers, as this appeared from them in many situations,

[Page 93]

such as their saying ﴿If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11], and ﴿When they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are misguided"﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 32], and (﴿So you took them in mockery until they made you forget My remembrance, while you used to laugh at them﴾) [al-Mu'minun: 110].

The two relative pronouns refer to two groups, as His saying about one of them indicates: ﴿and they followed their desires﴾.

Al-bayyina (the clear proof) means the evidence and the argument, that is, a proof that he is upon the truth.

The (min, "from") is for the starting point (ibtida'iyya). In expressing the Lord by the description and by attributing Him to the pronoun of the group, there is an alert to the nearness to Allah of the group that held fast to the proof of Allah.

The meaning of describing the proof as being "from Allah" is that Allah guided them to it and stirred their minds, so they complied and grasped the truth. The argument is an argument in itself, and its being from the side of Allah is a purification of it, a removal of hesitation about it, and a completion of its indication, just as the difference is apparent between taking knowledge from one who is thoroughly versed in it and taking it from one who is weak in it, even if the latter is correct.

The (ʿalā, "upon") is for the figurative elevation that has the meaning of firm establishment, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] in Surat al-Baqarah.

This group is the believers, who are steadfast in the religion and confident that they are upon the truth. Therefore, they certainly have success in this world, because Allah facilitated its means for them. If they fight, they do so with confidence that they are upon the truth and that they will attain one of the two good outcomes (husnayayn), so their courage is strengthened. If they make peace, they take care of managing their affairs and what benefits the community and the religion, and they spare no effort in doing good deeds. This is among the effects of Allah having set their affairs right and guided them.

The group for whom the evil of their deeds has been made attractive are the polytheists, for they were in states of evil, from worshipping idols, wrongdoing, transgression, and committing abominations. When Allah alerted them to the corruption of their deeds by sending to them a messenger who made clear to them the righteous deeds and their evil ones, they did not perceive this, and they saw their corruption as righteousness. Thus their deeds were made attractive in their eyes, they were unable to abandon them, and understanding and their desires overcame their judgment, so they did not heed following what was good for them in the immediate and the ultimate. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿like one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive, while they follow their desires﴾, in brief.

The verb "zuyyina" (was made attractive) is built in the passive so that it includes those who made it attractive to them among the leaders of their disbelief, and also what their corrupt intellects adorned for them of their evil deeds, out of being deceived by habit, or following immediate pleasures,

[Page 94]

or seeking leadership. That is, someone adorned for him the evil of his deed. In this construction to the passive there is also an alert to them, so that they return to themselves and reflect on who has made the evil of their deeds attractive to them.

Since the adorning of their deeds for them impels them to persist in them, habituation and attachment to them develop from this, and they become desires they cannot abandon. He therefore followed with His saying ﴿and they followed their desires﴾.

The difference between the two groups is clear to the reasonable, reflective person, such that it is right to ask about the equivalence of the two groups in the manner of one who knows that equivalence is absent and who rebukes whoever might claim it.

The meaning of the absence of equivalence is a metonymy (kinaya) for superiority, and the excellence intended is evident, namely the group that was praised.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr) on Sūrah 47 (Muḥammad), verse 15**

﴿The likeness of the Garden promised to the God-conscious (al-muttaqūn) is: therein are rivers of water unchanging (ghayr āsin), and rivers of milk whose taste has not altered, and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of purified honey. For them therein is every kind of fruit, and forgiveness from their Lord. Is it like one who abides forever in the Fire, and is given boiling water to drink, which cuts their intestines to pieces?﴾

This is a *istiʾnāf bayānī* (an explanatory resumptive sentence), because the mention of the Garden in His words, ﴿Indeed, God admits those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [Muḥammad: 12], leaves the listener eager to hear a detailed description of some of its attributes. Since it was said that rivers flow beneath it, the listener may think these are rivers of water, because flowing rivers are the most excellent of the desirable features of gardens. When the description of the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers, and of what has been prepared for each of them, and the declaration of the contrast between their two states, was completed, the reins were turned to explaining what is in the Garden promised to the God-conscious. Among this, the explanation of the kinds of rivers was singled out. Since this is the position of the sentence, His words ﴿The likeness of the Garden﴾ are a subject (*mubtadaʾ*) whose predicate is omitted. The estimated meaning is: "what will be described," or "what will be recited to you," or "from what is recited to you."

His words ﴿Is it like one who abides forever in the Fire?﴾ are a new sentence, with an implied interrogative of denial (*istifhām inkārī*), indicated by what preceded it in His words ﴿Is one who stands upon clear proof from his Lord like one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him?﴾ [Muḥammad: 14].

[Page 95]

The estimated meaning is: "Is it like one who abides forever in the Fire?" The denial applies to the comparison, which has the meaning of equivalence.

It is also permissible that the sentence ﴿The likeness of the Garden﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for the sentence ﴿Is one who stands upon clear proof from his Lord﴾ [Muḥammad: 14]. In that case it falls within the scope of the interrogative of denial. The predicate is His words ﴿like one who abides forever in the Fire﴾, meaning: "like the state of one who abides forever in the Fire." This requires that the state of the Fire differs from the state of the Garden. Thus there occurs what is called *iḥtibāk* (a rhetorical device in which each part omits what the other part states): ﴿The likeness of the Garden﴾ indicates the likeness of its people, and the likeness of one who abides in the Fire indicates the likeness of the Fire.

The purpose is to show the vast gap between the states of the Muslims and the polytheists, by mentioning the disparity between the two outcomes that was established in His words ﴿Indeed, God admits those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens﴾ [Muḥammad: 12] to the end of the verse. For this reason, He did not leave out mention of the people of the Garden and the people of the Fire in the midst of mentioning the Garden and the Fire. So He said ﴿The likeness of the Garden promised to the God-conscious﴾, and after it He said ﴿Is it like one who abides forever in the Fire?﴾

To intensify the depiction of the obstinacy of one who equates the one who holds fast to the clear proof of his Lord with the one who follows his own desires, the meaning is: he too is like one who equates the Garden, with those attributes, to the Fire, with attributes opposite to them.

In this verse is also the consistency of the sūrah's methods, for it opens with a contrast between those who disbelieved and those who believed, is followed by the disbelievers' following of falsehood and the believers' following of truth, and is given a third element in His words ﴿Is one who stands upon clear proof from his Lord﴾ [Muḥammad: 14], and so on.

*Al-mathal* means: a strange or remarkable state.

The clause ﴿therein are rivers﴾ and what is conjoined to it is a detailed explanation of the generality contained in the clause ﴿The likeness of the Garden﴾. So it is either a resumptive sentence, or a detailed substitute (*badal mufaṣṣal*) for a general term, according to the view of those who affirm this type of substitution among the kinds of *badal*.

*Al-anhār* is the plural of *nahr*, which is abundant water flowing in a great trench in the earth. It was discussed earlier in His words, exalted is He, ﴿He said: God will test you with a river﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249], in Sūrat al-Baqarah.

[Page 96]

As for applying the word "rivers" to rivers of water, it is literal usage (*ḥaqīqa*). As for applying "rivers" to what is of milk, wine, and honey, that is according to the method of *tashbīh baligh* (eloquent simile), meaning: a likeness to rivers. It is possible that the likeness is complete, in that they are like rivers, abundant in trenches in the earth of the Garden, since the states of the Hereafter transcend the familiar customs of this world, and the sight of rivers of these kinds is a delightful sight. It is also possible that the likeness of these kinds to rivers is in some of the attributes of rivers, namely their abundance (*istibḥār*).

These five kinds mentioned in the verse were among the finest things they competed for and among the most precious things that were readily obtainable. How much more so, then, is abundance of them, and even more so when rivers of them are in the Garden. And partaking of these kinds belongs to *tafakkuh* (enjoyment of fruits and delicacies), which is the luxury of the affluent and the comfortable.

Here four kinds of drinks are mentioned, which are the kinds of drinks they had. They prized clear water, because most of their water came from pools and basins in the desert, filled with rainwater or with the passing of torrents. When it stood for days, it began to change through algae and through what entered it from hands and buckets and the drinking of wild animals. Few were the lands neighboring flowing rivers.

Likewise milk: when they milked and drank, they preserved what remained for another time, because they milked only once or twice a day, and so a change would occur in the taste of the milk.

As for wine, it was scarce and precious among them, due to the scarcity of grapes in the Ḥijāz except for a little in al-Ṭāʾif. Wine was therefore imported from the lands of Syria and the lands of Yemen. It was very expensive, and its importation might be cut off for a time in winter because of the difficulty of travel by road, and also at times of war for fear of its being plundered.

Honey was also among their drinks. God, exalted is He, said about the bee: ﴿From their bellies comes a drink of varying colors﴾ [al-Naḥl: 69]. The Arabs say: "He gave him honey to drink" (*saqāhu ʿasalan*), and they say: "He fed him honey" (*aṭʿamahu ʿasalan*). Honey was desired, and was imported from mountainous lands of lasting vegetation.

As for fruits, some of them were abundant among them, like dates, and some were scarce, like pomegranates.

*Al-āsin* is an adjective derived from *asana al-māʾ*, of the patterns *ḍaraba*, *naṣara*, and *faraḥa*, meaning: when the water's color has changed. Ibn Kathīr recited it as *Asin* without an *alif* after the *hamza*, on the pattern *faʿil*, for emphasis (*mubālagha*).

[Page 97]

*Al-khamr* is the juice of grapes left until fermentation reaches it, which is sourness, like the leaven of dough.

*Ladhdha* is an adjective, not a noun. It is the feminine form of *al-ladhdh*, meaning *al-ladhīdh* (delicious). Bashshār said:

*I recalled my youth, its pleasure not far off, and a gathering of amusement, pleasant amid the drinking.*

*Al-ladhādha* is a psychological state containing pleasure, and it is the opposite of pain. Its occurrence is most frequent through tastes, drinks, and bodily touches. So describing the wine here as "delicious" means that its drinker finds delight in its taste. That is unlike the wine of this world, which is burning to the taste; were it not for anticipating what it does to the drinker of intoxication and elation, one would not drink it because of the sourness of its taste.

*Al-ʿasal al-muṣaffā* is honey that has been purified of what mixes with honey, such as remnants of wax and parts of the bees' bodies that may die in it. The discussion of honey and its production was given earlier in Sūrat al-Naḥl.

The meaning of ﴿of every kind of fruit﴾ is: kinds from all the species of fruits. So the definite article in "the fruits" is generic (*lil-jins*), and *kull* ("every") is used in its literal sense, which is comprehensiveness: all that God created of fruits, both what they knew in this world and what they did not know, which God created for the Garden. *Min* ("of") is partitive, and this is like His words ﴿In both of them are two kinds of every fruit﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 52].

*Maghfira* ("forgiveness") is conjoined to "rivers" and what follows it, meaning: and therein is forgiveness for them, that is, pardon for them, that is, permission regarding their deeds, with no obligation upon them, like His forgiveness of the people of Badr, as explained in the ḥadīth: "Perhaps God looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you." Forgiveness may also be a metaphor (*kināya*) for His good pleasure with them, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿And the good pleasure from God is greater﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72].

The omission of the modifier in "its likeness" is evident from the context.

His words ﴿And they are given boiling water to drink﴾ are brought in to contrast with what was described of the state of the people of the Garden in His words ﴿therein are rivers of water unchanging﴾ up to ﴿of every kind of fruit﴾. The meaning is that the people of the Fire are deprived of all the drinks mentioned. They taste nothing except the boiling water

[Page 98]

that cuts their intestines to pieces as soon as it is given to them. For this reason the verse does not turn aside here to the food of the people of the Fire, which is mentioned in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed you will eat from a tree of zaqqūm﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 52], ﴿and fill your bellies with it﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 53], ﴿then drink upon it from the boiling water﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 54], and His words ﴿Is that better as a hospitable meal, or the tree of zaqqūm?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 62], up to His words ﴿Indeed they will eat from it and fill their bellies from it﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 66], ﴿then indeed for them over it is a mixture of boiling water﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 67].

The pronoun in *suqū* ("they were given to drink") refers to "one who abides forever in the Fire," in view of the meaning of *man* ("one who"), which is the group of disbelievers, after the singular pronoun in His words ﴿he abides forever﴾ had been returned to it.

*Al-amʿāʾ* is the plural of *maʿan* (with a shortened form, and with the *mīm* pronounced with either a *fatḥa* or a *kasra*). It is what food passes into after descending from the stomach. It is called *ʿafaj*, on the pattern of *kitf*.

[Page 99]

The pronoun in *wa-minhum* ("and among them") refers to "those who disbelieved," who have been mentioned more than once since the beginning of the surah. That is, among the disbelievers there are people who listen to you. By "those who listen with them," he means the hypocrites (*munafiqun*), as indicated by His words ﴿they say to those who were given knowledge, "What did he say just now?"﴾ and by His words ﴿when they go out from your presence﴾.

The intended meaning is not merely those who listen, as in His words ﴿And among them are those who listen to you. Can you make the deaf hear?﴾ [Yunus: 42], and His words ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed veils over their hearts﴾ [al-An'am: 25]. This is because of the clear difference between the two styles. Rather, this is another category of disbelievers, those who concealed their disbelief and displayed faith. After the Hijrah, the hypocrites were intended by the term "disbelievers." This surah was revealed shortly after the Hijrah, so both groups of disbelievers are mentioned in it.

The meaning of ﴿they listen to you﴾ is that they attend your assembly, hear your speech, and hear what you recite to them of the Qur'an. This is the description of one who displays Islam, so they do not turn away from hearing the Qur'an in the manner of the polytheists in Makkah. It is narrated from al-Kalbi (*al-Kalbi*) and Muqatil (*Muqatil*) that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah

[Page 99 continues]
ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Rifa'ah ibn al-Tabut, al-Harith ibn 'Amr, Zayd ibn al-Salt, and Malik ibn al-Dakhshum.

*Al-istima'* (listening) means the most intense and strongest hearing. That is, they listen with concern, showing that they are eager to understand what the Messenger (ﷺ) says, and that they give him their full attention. This is the use of the verb to mean displaying the action rather than its actual occurrence. The verb *istama'a* should normally take its object directly, as in His words ﴿they listen to the Qur'an﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29]. When its connection to the person being listened to is intended, one says *istama'a ila fulan*, as He said here ﴿and among them are those who listen to you﴾. It occurs in this form in all its occurrences in the Qur'an.

The *ha'* (*hatta*) in His words ﴿until, when they go out from your presence﴾ is *ibtida'iyyah* (introductory), and *idha* is a temporal noun connected to "they said."

The meaning is: "So when they go out from your presence, they say..." etc.

*Al-khuruj* (going out) is leaving a specific place, whether confined or not. From it is His words ﴿when He brought me out of the prison﴾ [Yusuf: 100], and from it is His words ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾ [al-A'raf: 110].

Going out from the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ) is leaving his assembly in the mosque, which is what is expressed here by the phrase "from your presence."

The *min* in *kharajuu* is to make the verb transitive; it is not the *min* that is added with adverbs, as in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿from the presence of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79].

Those who were given knowledge (*alladhina utu al-'ilm*) are the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who were constant in attending his assembly. Among them, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Darda', and Ibn 'Abbas are named. It is narrated from him (Ibn Mas'ud) that he said: "I am among them," and he was asked about those who were asked.

The meaning is that they listen to the Prophet (ﷺ) recite the Qur'an and what he says of guidance. The object of *yastami'* is omitted so that it includes all of that.

[Page 100]

The meaning of *anifan* is: a time close to the time of speaking. This word does not occur except in the accusative as an adverb of time. Al-Zajjaj (*al-Zajjaj*) said: "It is derived from *ista'nafa al-shay'* when one begins something," meaning that it is derived from a derived verb, and no unaugmented verb has been heard for it. The apparent sense of their statements is that its derivation is from the solid noun *al-anf* (the nose), that is, the organ of smell. They seem to have meant the nose of a camel, because the nose is the first thing that appears to its rider, so he takes hold of its halter. Thus the notion of appearing was seen in the noun *anf*, and this was used as a metaphor for nearness. Others said: "It is derived from *unuf*, with *damma* on the *hamza* and *damma* on the *nun*, which is used to describe a cup from which no one has drunk before, and a meadow that has not been grazed before." It seems they noticed in it the necessary implication of the description of non-use, which is newness, that is, a recent time. So *anifan* means a time whose recency has not passed. Ibn 'Atiyyah (*Ibn 'Atiyyah*) said: "The exegetes say: *anifan* means: the hour close to us." This is an explanation of the meaning. There is an objection to his statement, because the lexicographers explained it as a time that is close to us.

It is formed on the pattern of the active participle, but it does not have the meaning of the active participle. This is an unusual word in morphology, and no line of Arabic poetry is known in which this word occurs.

The reciters agreed on reading it in the form *fa'il*. A narration from al-Bazzi (*al-Bazzi*) from Ibn Kathir (*Ibn Kathir*) is anomalous (*shadhdhah*), that he read *anifan* on the pattern of *kitf*. Some scholars of the readings (*qira'at*) denied the attribution of this to Ibn Kathir, but al-Shatibi (*al-Shatibi*) recorded it in *Hirz al-Amani*, and Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) mentioned it in *al-Hujjah*.

If this narration from al-Bazzi from him is sound, then *anifan* is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of the pronoun in ﴿who listens﴾, treated in the singular in observance of the wording of *man*. Its meaning is that he says that in a state of being extremely disdainful (*al-anafah*), that is, arrogance, displaying his elevation above understanding what the Prophet (ﷺ) says. The sentence ends at "what." Abu 'Ali in *al-Hujjah* claimed that al-Bazzi imagined it to be like *hadhir* and *hadhar*. Such a thing should not be attributed to al-Bazzi if the narration from him from Ibn Kathir is sound.

The context of the speech indicates a disparagement of this question, by His words following it ﴿those are the ones whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts﴾. So it is a question that reveals the blameworthiness of those who ask it. If their question was genuine, it reveals their lack of understanding of what they hear from the Prophet (ﷺ), so they ask those who knew it to repeat it. Perhaps their asking it again was for the purpose of studying it together when they are alone with their companions, to invent schemes they prepare among themselves, or to answer those of their companions who ask them what they heard in the assembly they were in.

[Page 101]

It is also possible that the question was not genuine, but intended as mockery, displaying to the believers their concern to repeat what they heard, and saying to their companions: "We are only mocking." Or their question may have been an implicit insinuation that they heard speech whose intended meaning was not clear, to introduce doubt into the souls of those whom they sense desire to attend the assemblies of the Prophet (ﷺ), as an indirect hint at the little benefit of attending them.

It is also possible that the verse refers to a specific incident in which the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned the hypocrites and their conditions, and those among them who were present knew that they were the ones meant. So they wanted to ask a question seeking information: whether those with knowledge had perceived that those were the ones meant. In that case, the object of *yastami'un* is omitted, because it is known to the Prophet (ﷺ).

* * *

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts and who followed their desires﴾

This is an *istinaf bayani* (explanatory resumptive sentence), because their saying ﴿what did he say just now?﴾ is a strange question that naturally provokes the question of someone asking about the cause of their arriving, under all the previous assumptions, at their intention from it.

The demonstrative noun was used after mentioning their attributes to make them notorious. The relative pronoun and its clause were used as a predicate of the demonstrative, to convey that these people distinguished by these attributes are actual members of the group known among people as a group sealed upon their hearts. This is because it is established among Muslims that those who insist on disbelief are those whose hearts Allah has sealed and who follow their desires. So this conveys that these listeners are a band from that group. This construction follows the style of His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Those are the successful﴾ [al-A'raf: 157] in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Al-tab' 'ala al-qalb* (sealing upon the heart) is a metaphor for the non-mixing of guidance and right direction with their minds, like the state of a sealed book or a sealed vessel, such that whoever tries to reach its inside cannot reach it. So the meaning is that Allah created their hearts, that is, their minds, unable to perceive and affirm the realities and guidance. This sealing varies: part of it leaves some of its people after varying periods, and part of it persists with some until death, as has occurred. Its removal happens when the veil of misguidance on the mind ends, and when Allah's kindness (*lutf*) turns toward whomever He wills by His wisdom. This kindness is called *tawfiq* (divine enabling), which the Ash'ariyyah (*Ash'ariyyah*, followers of al-Ash'ari) explained as the creation of the power and motive toward obedience, and as that which, when it occurs to a servant, results in his well-being in the Hereafter. The Mu'tazilah (*Mu'tazilah*) explained *lutf* as conveying benefits to the servant in a way whose perception is subtle, and enabling him with power and tools.

The commentary is the sentence ﴿And those who were guided — He increased them in guidance and granted them their God-consciousness﴾ and it is an interpolated clause (*jumlah mu'tarida*, a parenthetical clause) placed between the sentence ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [Muhammad: 16] and what is understood from His words ﴿Are they waiting for anything but the Hour?﴾ [Muhammad: 18]. The waw is parenthetical (*i'tiradiyyah*).

The purpose of this interpolation is to contrast the party of misguidance with the party of guidance, following the method upon which this surah was constructed, as was mentioned at its beginning. This method is continuous, even though the positions of its sentences vary.

The meaning: those whose breasts God expanded for faith and who were guided, God's kindness toward them increased them in guidance, firmly established faith in their hearts, and enabled them to attain taqwa (God-consciousness), so they guarded themselves and overcame their desires.

The granting of taqwa is a metaphor for facilitating its causes, since taqwa is a psychological state, whereas granting (*iyta'*) properly applies to concrete entities.

The attribution of taqwa to the pronoun in ﴿those who were guided﴾ [Maryam: 76] indicates that they were known for it and that it was specific to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 18:

﴿So do they await anything but the Hour, that it come upon them suddenly? But its signs have already come.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of what preceded concerning the description of the states of the disbelievers, from His saying ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth?﴾ [Muhammad: 10] up to His saying ﴿and followed their desires﴾ [Muhammad: 16], which encompasses the states of both groups. From this he derives that both groups await the arrival of the Hour, so that they may receive their recompense for the evil of their disbelief. The pronoun in "yanzurun" (they await) refers to the disbelievers, because the speech is a threat and a warning, and because the believers await other matters, such as victory and martyrdom. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Do you await for us anything but one of the two best things?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 52], and so on. The word "nazar" here carries the meaning of "intizar" (waiting), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels come to them, or that your Lord comes?﴾ [al-An'am: 158], and so on.

The interrogation is a denial (inkar) mixed with mockery (tahakkum), and it is a denial and mockery directed at absent persons, addressed to the Messenger ﷺ. That is: do not reckon that the delay of their punishment is an escape from retribution, for they are deferred until the Hour.

This denying interrogation looks back to His saying earlier: ﴿And those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as the cattle eat, and the Fire is their abode﴾ [Muhammad: 12].

The restriction (qasr) conveyed by the exception is a claimed (idda'i) restriction: their waiting for what they hope for of worldly desirables has been placed in the position of non-existence, because its matter is insignificant, after they have been placed in the position of those who await, among what they await, the Hour; for, since its arrival upon them is certain, they are deserving of being among those who await it.

And ﴿that it come upon them﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "the Hour."

And "baghtatan" (suddenly) is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "the Hour," as in His saying: ﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]. "Baghtah" means sudden onset (al-faja'ah), and it is a verbal noun carrying the meaning of a single occurrence; what is meant here is the attribute, that is, surprising them.

The meaning of the speech is: the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is near to them. Their situation is like that of one who waits for something; waiting occurs only when the appointed time of a thing draws near. This metaphor is a mocking one (tahakkumiyyah).

The fa' in His saying ﴿but its signs have already come﴾ is the fa' of eloquence (fa' al-fasihah), like the one in the verse of 'Abbas ibn al-Ahnaf:

They said: Khurasan is the farthest that we are aimed at, then the return. So we have come, to Khurasan.

This fa' conveys the meaning of giving the reason for the nearness of their punishment.

"Ashrat" is the plural of "shart" (with two fathas), and it means a sign or indicator of the existence of a thing or of its attribute.

The signs of the Hour are the signs of its being near. This nearness is conceived in two ways. The first: the time of the Hour is near in relative terms, in comparison with the long duration of this world and of the creatures upon it.

The second: the beginning of witnessing the states of the Hour occurs for each person at his death, for when his soul separates from his body it witnesses its destination in a general way. It is in this sense that the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raised (marfu') to the Prophet, is interpreted: "The grave is a garden of the gardens of Paradise, or a pit of the pits of the Fire." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi. It is weak, and it is explained by the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, raised to the Prophet: "When the dead person dies, his seat is displayed to him morning and evening; if he is of the people of Paradise, then he is of the people of Paradise, and if he is of the people of the Fire, then he is of the people of the Fire. Then it is said: This is your seat, until Allah resurrects you on the Day of Resurrection." The end of a person's life is near, even if his lifespan is long.

As for the signs in relation to the first aspect: they are the events which the Prophet ﷺ informed would occur before the Hour, the first of which is his own mission, for he is the last of the Messengers and his law is the last of the laws, and then what comes after that. As for the signs in relation to the second aspect: they are sicknesses and old age.

* * *
﴿So how will they have their reminder when it has come to them?﴾

This is a consequence of ﴿but its signs have already come﴾. "Anna" is a noun indicating a state, and it is often used with the meaning of interrogation; here it is a denying interrogation, that is: how will reminder be attained by them when the Hour comes upon them? The intended meaning is the denial of benefiting from the reminder at that time.

"Anna" is the second, fronted predicate (mubtada' thani muqaddam), since interrogation has the priority of position. "Dhikra-hum" is the first subject (mubtada' awwal), and "lahum" is the predicate concerning "anna." This construction is like His saying: ﴿How will they have the reminder?﴾ [al-Dukhan: 13] in Surat al-Dukhan. The pronoun in "jaat-hum" refers to the Hour.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 19:

﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah, and ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women. And Allah knows your movement and your resting place.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') drawn from everything that was mentioned about the state of the believers, the state of the disbelievers, and the outcomes of each, with its promise or its threat. Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to remain steadfast in what he already knows of the Oneness of Allah, and in what is his constant practice of humility before Allah, by asking forgiveness for his own sin, and of eagerness for the salvation of the believers, by asking forgiveness for them. This is because in that knowledge and that practice lies the drawing down of good things for him and for his community.

صفحة ١٠٥
This consequence adds further relevance to His saying earlier: ﴿That is because Allah is the Protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector﴾ [Muhammad: 11], and so on.

The imperative in His saying (fa-'lam, "so know") is a metaphorical expression (kinayah) for requesting knowledge, and knowledge here means acting upon what is known. This usage is employed to request its continuance, because the Prophet ﷺ already knew this and the believers knew it too. When this knowledge has been attained once, it becomes firmly fixed in the soul, since knowledge does not admit its opposite. So the command to it, after it has been attained, is not a command to seek its acquisition, but a command to seek steadfastness in it. It is thus like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [An-Nisa: 136].

As for the imperative in His saying ﴿and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾, it is a request to renew that, if the Prophet ﷺ had known it and acted upon it before; or it is a request to attain it, if he had not done so before.

The mention of "the believing women" (al-mu'minat) after "the believing men" (al-mu'minin) is an emphasis on them in this context. Otherwise, the Qur'an generally suffices with mentioning the believers, and its scope includes the believing women by way of taghlib (predominance of the masculine form), since it is known that the obligations of the Sharia apply to men and women alike, except where something has been excepted from the obligations.

Among the Qur'anic subtleties is that here He commanded knowledge before the command to action, in His saying ﴿and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾. Ibn 'Uyaynah said, when he was asked about the excellence of knowledge: "Have you not heard His saying when He began with it: ﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah, and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾?" Al-Bukhari, in the Book of Knowledge of his Sahih, titled a chapter "Knowledge before speech and action," citing the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah﴾, thus beginning with knowledge.

What the Prophet ﷺ asks forgiveness for is not among the evil deeds, since he is protected from them (ismah). Rather, it is seeking forgiveness for heedlessness (ghaflat) and the like. His being described as having a "sin" in the verse is either an imitation of what the Prophet ﷺ used to frequently say, "O Allah, forgive me my error" (Allahumma-ghfir li khati'ati), which he said in a state of humility; or it is an application of the name "sin" to what escapes one of increased worship, such as the times of sleep and eating; and its application to what the Prophet ﷺ meant in his saying: "Indeed, there is a veil over my heart, and indeed I seek forgiveness from Allah a hundred times a day."

صفحة ١٠٦
The lam in His saying "li-dhanbika" (for your sin) is the lam of specification (lam al-ta'yin), clarifying the second object of the verb "istaghfir" (ask forgiveness). The lam in His saying "wa-lil-mu'minin" (and for the believers) is the lam of cause (lam al-'illah), or it has the meaning of "'an" (concerning), and the object is omitted, meaning: ask forgiveness of sins for the sake of the believers. There is an ellipsis in the speech, its estimated form being: "and for the believers, [ask forgiveness] for their sins."

The clause ﴿And Allah knows your movement and your resting place﴾ is a comprehensive conclusion (tadhyil) encompassing the states of what preceded. The word "mutaqallab" is a verbal noun meaning "turning about" (taqallub); it was chosen here to pair with His saying "and your resting place." Taqallub means action that varies, whether outwardly, such as prayer, or inwardly, such as faith and sincere counsel.

Mathwa means the place of return and ultimate end. That is, Allah knows the states of all of you, believers and disbelievers, and He has decreed for each its recompense according to His knowledge of its levels, and He knows your destinies. He commanded and forbade you, and commanded you to seek forgiveness specifically, so that the rulings of causes apply to their effects, so do not despair and do not neglect.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 20:

﴿And those who believe say, "Why has a surah not been sent down?" But when a clear surah is sent down and fighting is mentioned in it, you see those in whose hearts is a disease looking at you with the look of one fainting from death. So woe to them.﴾ ﴿Obedience and right speech.﴾ [Muhammad: 21]

We have mentioned that this surah was revealed in Madinah, when the buds of the hypocrites' (munafiqun) hypocrisy had appeared. When the description of the state of the hypocrites occurred in this surah, it was followed by a description of the most manifest signs of their hypocrisy, and that is when the Muslims are called to jihad. The matter becomes distressing for the hypocrites, since their outward profession of Islam will compel them to go out to fight alongside the Muslims. This is no small matter, for it exposes them to the destruction of their souls without hoping for any benefit from it in the everlasting life, since they do not affirm it, so they remain in bewilderment. Their state was contrary to the state of those who believed, who wished that the Qur'an would descend with a call to fighting so that they might meet the polytheists and cool their burning rage against them. Because of this occasion, the wish of the believers for the descent of the command of fighting is related, for it reveals the distinction of the state of the hypocrites and shows the difference between the states of the two groups. He has already made clear their aversion to fighting in Surat Bara'ah.

The purpose of this verse is His saying ﴿But when a clear surah is sent down and fighting is mentioned in it, you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, and what precedes it is a preface to it by mentioning its cause. Placing it first also serves to honour those who believe, and mentioning it provides a contrast between the states of the two groups, in keeping with the customs of this surah. The statement of these believers was the cause of the revelation of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, then [it is] striking of the necks﴾ [Muhammad: 4]. Therefore, the surah in which fighting is mentioned, meant here, is this very surah we are discussing.

It is known that this statement of the believers occurred before the descent of this verse, so its expression with the present tense is either for the purpose of bringing the situation vividly to mind, like ﴿and he was constructing the ark﴾ [Hud: 38], or to indicate that they were persistent in this statement.

Accordingly, (idha) in His saying ﴿But when a clear surah is sent down﴾ is an adverb used for past time, because the descent of the surah has already taken place, and the look of the hypocrites at the Messenger (ﷺ) in this manner has already occurred, since their censure and rebuke cannot occur before what necessitates it has taken place. The context indicates it and the indication is clear.

(Law) [lawla] here is a particle used to express wishing. Its original meaning is restriction, so it is used and intended to express wishing, because wishing entails eagerness, and eagerness calls for urging.

The description "surah" is omitted in the quotation of their statement ﴿Why has a surah not been sent down?﴾ because what follows it indicates it, namely His saying ﴿and fighting is mentioned in it﴾, because His saying ﴿But when a surah is sent down﴾, i.e., as they wished, requires that what is requested is a surah in which fighting against the polytheists is legislated. The meaning is: "Why has a surah not been sent down in which fighting and its obligation are mentioned?" So the description is omitted for brevity.

Describing the surah as ﴿clear (muhkamah)﴾ is by reference to its verses being described as clear, i.e., free from ambiguity and without the possibility of other meanings, as indicated by the contrast of the clear verses (muhkamat) with the ambiguous ones (mutashabihat) in His saying ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are clear (muhkamat), they are the foundation of the Book, and others that are ambiguous (mutashabihat)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7] in Surat Al 'Imran. That is, the verses of that surah concerning fighting admit of nothing but the obligation of fighting and the absence of leniency in it, like His saying ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, then [it is] striking of the necks﴾ [Muhammad: 4] and the verses that follow. Undoubtedly, this surah is the one that descended in answer to the wish of those who believed.

He said ﴿and fighting is mentioned in it﴾ because the surah is not entirely devoted to the mention of fighting, for the surahs of the Qur'an have various purposes.

The address in "you see" (ra'ayta) is to the Prophet (ﷺ), because it follows His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [Muhammad: 16].

And ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ are those who conceal disbelief. He made hidden disbelief like a disease whose seat is the heart, from which nothing appears on the outward body. That is, you see the hypocrites by way of metaphor. This relative clause has become predominantly applied to the hypocrites, and hypocrisy is an inner, grave sickness, since many branches arise from it, which we have explained in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿in their hearts is a disease﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

The phrase ﴿the look of one fainting from death﴾ is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) explaining the manner of the look in ﴿look at you﴾, so it carries the meaning of an eloquent simile.

The point of resemblance is the fixedness of the pupil and the absence of its movement, i.e., they look at you with the look of one bewildered, directed in a single direction, not occupied with visible things because he is preoccupied away from looking. They direct their gaze at the Prophet (ﷺ) because they were in his gathering at the time of the surah's descent, and they used to feign attentiveness to receiving what he uttered of the revelation. But when they heard the mention of fighting, they were stunned. So the intended meaning is the resemblance in this image. And in the sense of this verse is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿But when fear comes, you see them looking at you, their eyes rolling like one over whom there has come a swoon of death﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19] in Surat al-Ahzab.

Here (min) is causal, i.e., fainting due to death, that is, the presence of death.

Upon this is based His saying ﴿So woe to them﴾ ﴿obedience and right speech﴾ [Muhammad: 21].

This branching is a parenthetical insertion between the clause ﴿they look at you with the look of one fainting from death﴾ and the clause ﴿But when the matter is resolved﴾ [Muhammad: 21].

The word (awla) here may be used in its apparent sense as a comparative of preference over something unmentioned, indicated by what precedes it, i.e., "more fitting for them than that fear which their look, like one fainting from death, indicates: that they obey God and say a right word, which is 'We hear and we obey'." That right word among the believers, when they are called or commanded, is as He, exalted is He, said ﴿The saying of the believers, when they are called to God and His Messenger to judge between them, is only that they say, "We hear and we obey"﴾ [al-Nur: 51] in Surat al-Nur.

On this interpretation, the construction of (awla) with (li-) rather than (bi-) indicates that this is more fitting and more beneficial, so the bringing in of the lam serves to indicate the sense of benefit. It is like His saying ﴿That is purer for you﴾ [al-Nur: 30] and His saying ﴿These are purer for you﴾ [Hud: 78].

It is connected to His following saying ﴿But if they were true to God, it would be better for them﴾ [Muhammad: 21].

It is also possible that ﴿So woe to them﴾ is used in the sense of threat and warning, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Woe to you, and woe﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 34] ﴿Again, woe to you, and woe﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 35] in Surat al-Qiyamah. This is the interpretation Zamakhshari confined himself to. Its meaning is that God informed of His threat against them.

Then it was said on this interpretation that "awla," whose letters remain in their original form, is derived from al-Wali, which means nearness, and that its pattern is af'al. Al-Jurjani said that in this usage it is derived from al-Wayl (woe), so the original of awla is awyal, meaning "more woeful," and a metathesis occurred in it, and its pattern is af'al. In the Sihah, from al-Asma'i, there is what indicates that he takes "awla lahu" as a subject with an omitted predicate. The estimate is: "nearest to destroying him." Tha'lab said: "No one has said anything better about 'awla lahu' than what al-Asma'i said."

The lam on this interpretation is either superfluous, meaning God has made befall them what they dislike, and it is like the lam in the words of al-Nabigha:

"Watering and pasturing for that blamer, the reproacher"

Or it is connected to (awla) as a past-tense verb, and on this usage His saying ﴿obedience and right speech﴾ [Muhammad: 21] is a resumed statement, and it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "obedience and right speech are better for them," or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, estimated as: "the matter is obedience and right speech," i.e., God commanded that they obey.

[Page 110]

﴿So when the matter is resolved upon, if they had been true to God, it would have been better for them.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the description of the hypocrites' state of panic at the mention of fighting. When the matter of fighting becomes serious, that is, when the time comes for the Muslims to be called to fight, the hypocrites' affairs will be thrown into confusion, and they will slip away, hiding behind one another, from attending the struggle (jihad). The better course for them at that time would be to make their faith sincere and to strive as the sincere Muslims strive. Otherwise, they have no escape from one of two outcomes: either they attend the fighting without intention, and then defeat will befall them and they will lose themselves in vain, or they will withdraw from fighting, as Ibn Ubayy and his followers did on the day of Uhud.

"Idha" (when) is a adverb of future time, which is its most common use, so what follows it is presumed to be yet to occur. That is, "when the matter of fighting becomes serious and takes place."

The clause ﴿if they had been true to God﴾ is the response (jawab) that stands in for the apodosis of "idha," because "idha" here carries the meaning of a conditional particle. That is, they lied to God and broke their word, so if they had been true to God, it would have been better for them. The connection of the response clause with "fa" (then) indicates that "idha" has the sense of a condition. This is better than omitting the "fa," when the response clause is itself conditional.

The definite article in "al-amr" (the matter) is the definite article of prior reference, or the "lam" substituting for the genitive. That is, the matter of fighting mentioned just before, in His saying ﴿And when fighting is mentioned in it﴾ [Muhammad: 20].

"Al-'azm" means resolution and the certainty of a matter, that is, that it is unavoidable.

The verb "'azama" (to resolve) is used figuratively for determination and necessity, by way of the metaphor in the implicit form (al-makniyya), by likening "the matter," meaning fighting, to a man who has resolved upon some action. Ascribing resolve to it is an imaginative device (takhyiliyya), like ascribing claws to death. This is the method of al-Sakkaki (d. 626 AH) in all examples of the rational metaphor (al-majaz al-'aqli). It is a subtle method, but not consistently applicable; it is used when the context permits it.

In al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary), the attribution of "resolve" to "the matter" is made a rational metaphor, its real attribution being to the people who resolve, according to the common practice in such cases. Here, however, this is far-fetched, since the meaning does not concern the seriousness arising from the people concerned with the matter. A parallel is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, that is of the determined matters﴾ [Luqman: 17], and the discussion regarding it is the same.

[Page 111]

The meaning of ﴿they had been true to God﴾ is that they would speak truth to Him, which is the agreement of speech with what is in reality, that is, if they had been truthful in their saying: "We are believers." They only lied to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when they showed him the opposite of what was in their souls. So He made lying to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) equivalent to lying to God, to express its enormity and to magnify its consequence. That is, if they had made their faith sincere and fought with the intention of jihad, it would have been better for them in this world and the Hereafter. In this world, it would be the goodness of honour and dignity, and in the Hereafter, the goodness of Paradise.

This verse is thus a forewarning of what will come from them when the matter becomes serious and the time of fighting arrives. It is among the miracles of the Qur'an in its reports of the unseen. The matter of fighting became resolved on the day of Uhud, and the hypocrites went out with the Muslim army in the appearance of those who strive. When the army reached the place between Medina and Uhud, 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the chief of the hypocrites, said: "We do not know why we are killing ourselves here, O people!" He turned back with his followers, and they were a third of the army. That was in the third year after the Hijra, that is, about three years after the revelation of this verse.

His saying ﴿So if they had been true to God﴾ is the response, as previously explained. In the speech there is brevity (ijaz), because His saying ﴿it would have been better﴾ indicates that when the matter becomes resolved, there befalls them what has no good in it.

The word "khayran" (better) is the opposite of evil (sharr), of the pattern "fa'l," and it is not here of the pattern "af'al" (the comparative form).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 22:

﴿So is it likely that, if you turn away, you will cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾

The coherence of the arrangement (tanasuq al-nazm) requires that this is a consequence of His saying: ﴿But when the matter is resolved upon, if they had been true to Allah, it would have been better for them﴾ [Muhammad: 21]. This is because it is understood from it that when the matter is resolved upon, they turn away from fighting and their hypocrisy is exposed. Thus it completes what the preceding verse foretold about what the hypocrites would do on the day of Uhud. 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy had said: "Why should we kill ourselves here?" and perhaps he said in his speech: "How can we fight Quraysh when they are of our own people?" He did not consider it obligatory for the people of Yathrib to fight alongside the Prophet ﷺ, and he regarded it as sufficient that they had sheltered him. The address is directed to those in whose hearts is a disease, by way of iltifat (a shift from third person to second person).

The interrogative is used for rebuke (al-takdhib) concerning what they would offer as an excuse for their withdrawal. For this reason (hal), which indicates confirmation (al-tahqiq), is used with it, since in interrogation it holds the position of (qad) in declarative speech. The meaning is: "Will it be confirmed, if you turn away, that you will cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship, while you claim that you turned away out of concern for yourselves and for your close kin?" This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Is it likely that, if fighting is prescribed for you, you will not fight?" They said…﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246]. This is a rebuke, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you are those who kill your own selves and expel a group of you from their homes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85]. The meaning is: you fall into what you claimed to be avoiding, by supporting disbelief and creating enmity between yourselves and your people, the Ansar.

Here, tawalli (turning away) means returning from the direction in which they set out, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except a few of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246], and His saying: ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away?﴾ [al-Najm: 33], and His saying: ﴿Then Pharaoh turned away, gathered his scheme, and came﴾ [Ta-Ha: 60]. Ibn Jurayj and Qatadah explained it in this same way, though their explanations vary. Among the exegetes, some understood tawalli to be the intransitive form of walla, meaning to give someone authority (wilaya), i.e., the authority of rule and command over people. Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Kalbi and Ka'b al-Ahbar explained it this way. This is far from the wording and from the arrangement, and it severs the connection of the discourse and moves to another subject without any relevance. Some went further and claimed that it was revealed concerning the Kharijites. Others made it refer to what happens between the Banu Umayyah and the Banu Hashim, following the habit of the Shi'a and the factions of bending the Book of Allah to what it cannot bear and restricting its general terms to some of what is intended by them.

Nafi' alone read ﴿'asītum﴾ with a kasra on the sin, while the rest of the ten readers read it with a fatha on the sin. Both are dialectal forms of the verb 'asa when attached to a pronoun. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: The reason for the kasra is that its verb is 'asiya, like radiya, and they only pronounced it when this verb was attached to a pronoun. Attaching it to a pronoun is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz; as for the Banu Tamim, they never attach it to a pronoun at all, and they say: ʿasā an tafʿalū.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 23:

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, so He has made them deaf and blinded their vision.﴾

The reference to "those in whose hearts is a disease" follows the style of His saying earlier, ﴿Those are the ones upon whose hearts Allah has set a seal﴾ [Muhammad: 16]. It is not correct for the reference to be to what is understood from His saying ﴿that you would cause corruption in the land and sever your ties of kinship﴾ [Muhammad: 22], because that does not entail the curse, nor that those who commit it are in the position of the deaf. Moreover, the past-tense form in the verbs ﴿cursed﴾, ﴿made deaf﴾, and ﴿blinded﴾ does not accord with His saying ﴿Then would it be that if you turned away, you would cause corruption﴾ [Muhammad: 22], nor with the future time implied by the particle (in) ("if").

Deafness is used figuratively for not benefiting from what is heard of the verses of the Qur'an and the admonitions of the Prophet (ﷺ). Likewise, blindness is used here figuratively for lack of understanding, by way of metaphor (tamthil), because the condition of the blind man is to be disoriented regarding what surrounds him, not knowing what benefits him from what harms him except with the help of someone who guides him. It is common to say: "Allah has blinded his sight," meaning that He did not guide him. This is the point behind the wording ﴿and blinded their vision﴾ differing from the wording of ﴿so He made them deaf﴾, since it does not say "and blinded them."

The verse also implies that corruption in the land and severing of kinship ties are among the marks of the people of disbelief, and so these are two grave sins which the believers must avoid.

This is a consequence (*tafrī'*) of His saying: ﴿So He made them deaf and blinded their sight﴾ [Muhammad: 23]. That is, why do they not contemplate the Qur'an, instead of occupying their minds in your assembly by tracking the condition of the believers? Or it is a consequence of His saying: ﴿So He made them deaf and blinded their sight﴾ [Muhammad: 23].

The meaning is that God created them with minds that are not affected by the meanings of goodness and righteousness. So they do not contemplate the Qur'an while understanding it, or they do not understand it when they receive it. Both of these are strange.

The interrogative form (*istifhām*) expresses wonder at the poor state of their knowledge of the Qur'an and at their turning away from listening to it.

The particle *am* (أمْ) is for a transitional change of subject (*iḍrāb intiqālī*). The meaning is: "Rather, there are locks upon their hearts." This is the view followed by the majority of the exegetes, and it is what runs in line with Sibawayh's words in God's saying: ﴿Will you not then see?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 51] ﴿Or am I better than this one who is contemptible?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 52] in Surat al-Zukhruf. This is contrary to what Ibn Hisham appears to imply, or what he supposed, in *Mughni al-Labib*.

*Tadabbur* means reflecting on the inner meaning of a matter, that is, what is hidden within it. It is derived from *dubur al-shay'*, meaning the back or behind of a thing.

The word *aqfāl* is the plural of *qufl* (lock). It is a metaphor by implicit comparison (*istiʿāra makniyya*), since the hearts, meaning the minds in their failure to grasp the meanings, are likened to closed doors or sealed chests. The "locks" are an imaginative element (*takhyīl*), like the claws of death in the words of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

*And when death sinks its claws in, you will find that every amulet is useless.*

The indefinite form of "hearts" (*qulūb*) is for variety (*tanwīʿ*) or partiality (*tabʿīḍ*). That is, upon a kind of hearts there are locks. The meaning is: "Rather, some hearts have locks upon them." This is an indirect allusion (*taʿrīḍ*) that their hearts are of this kind, because affirming this kind of heart in the course of expressing wonder at their failure to contemplate the Qur'an implies, by necessary implication (*dalālat al-iltizām*), that their hearts belong to this kind of heart that has locks. So that their hearts are of this kind is derived from the transitional change of subject in describing their condition.

Close to this is the verse of Labid:

*Abandoner of places when I do not like them, or when death seizes some souls.*

He means himself, because it came after his saying "abandoner of places..." That is, "I am an abandoner of places."

The construction of *aqfāl* with the pronoun referring to *qulūb* is a wonderful composition (*naẓm badīʿ*). It points to the locks being specific to those hearts, meaning that they are constantly attached to them, and so it indicates that those hearts are hard.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, those who turned back on their heels after guidance had become clear to them—Satan has enticed them and given them false hope.﴾

The discussion has not ceased to concern the hypocrites, so "those who turned back on their heels" are hypocrites. It is possible that what is meant is a group among the people of hypocrisy who had truly believed and then returned to disbelief, because they were weak in faith and little at ease in their belief. These are the ones whom God described in Surat al-Baqara with His saying, ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire, and when it illuminated what was around him, God took away their light﴾ [al-Baqara: 17], and so on.

Turning back upon one's heels, in this sense, is a figurative expression for one who returns to disbelief after faith, by the condition of someone who travels to reach a place and then turns back on his way. Since turning back is a movement toward the direction behind the traveler, "turning back upon the heels," that is, toward the direction of the heels, is used. The particle (ʿalā, "upon") is used to indicate that the turning back is firmly established from the direction of the heels, as one says: ʿalā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm ("upon a straight path").

"Guidance" here means faith, and guidance becoming clear to them in this sense is a real clarification, because they did not believe except after the guidance of faith had become clear to them.

In this sense, the use of the relative pronoun with its clause is not a substitution of an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, because the people of this clause are some of those whom the discussion had concerned earlier.

It is also possible that what is meant is all the hypocrites, and that their persistence in disbelief after their sharing with the Muslims in their circumstances—in the gathering of the Prophet ﷺ, praying with him, hearing the Qur'an and the admonitions—is expressed by "turning back," because it is a departure from those good circumstances; that is, they returned to the words and deeds of disbelief, and that is when they were alone with their satans. The clarity of guidance in this sense means that it is clear in itself, and it is clear to them because of the evidence of its proofs, with no dust upon it. This clarity is of the same kind as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿That is the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqara: 2], that is, there is nothing with it that would necessitate the doubt of the doubters.

It is also possible that what is meant is a group of the hypocrites who did not fight alongside the Muslims after they knew that fighting was true. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. On this basis, the intended meaning is probably the group who withdrew on the day of Uhud with ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and "turning back upon the heels" in this sense is literal, because they turned back from the place of fighting after having arrived at it, and returned to Medina, with Medina behind them. This, in my view, is the stronger of the two views and the more fitting with His saying after it, ﴿That is because they said to those who hated what God had sent down: "We will obey you in part of the matter"﴾ [Muhammad: 26], down to His saying, ﴿and their backs﴾ [Muhammad: 27]. And guidance in this sense is the truth, that is, after they knew that the truth was fighting the polytheists.

The predicate of "inna" was chosen to be a sentence, so that the sentence might include the features of beginning with the name of Satan, for the sake of giving it attention in the purpose of censuring them, and so that a verbal predicate would be attributed to his name, to convey the strengthening of the judgment, like the saying: "He gives abundantly."

Taswil (enticement) is making easy a matter that is sensed to be difficult or harmful, and adorning what is not good. Imla' (giving respite) is extension and prolongation in time, and it is also used for leaving something in place for a long time; that is, He showed them that turning back was good, enduringly, as He related of him in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120]. That is, their turning back is from the work of Satan.

The majority read ﴿wa-amlā lahum﴾ with a fatha on the hamza, in the active voice. Abu ʿAmr read it with a damma on the hamza, a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the letter ya', in the passive voice. Ya'qub read it with a damma on the hamza, a kasra on the lam and a sukun on the letter ya', as attributed to the speaker, so the pronoun returns to God, exalted is He; that is, Satan enticed them and I give them respite, so the statement becomes a threat, meaning: I delay them a little, then I punish them.

﴿That is because they said to those who hated what God had sent down: "We will obey you in part of the matter," but God knows their secrets.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (*istiʼnaf bayani*, a sentence that answers an implied question). The implied question runs: how did Satan's enticement to apostasy after guidance had become clear to them actually manifest? The answer is that Satan lured them into error when guidance had become clear to them. He embellished for them the idea that they could side with the people of polytheism and disbelief in some matters, and he made them think that such agreement in part did not nullify their guidance. When they did side with them, they found sweetness in the disbelief they were accustomed to, in the matters where they had sided with the people of disbelief, so they began returning to the familiar disbelief until they "turned back on their heels." This is the way of the soul: it returns to what it loves after having abstained from it, if the abstention is recent.

So the meaning of "they said" (*qalū*) is that they said it as a statement arising from belief and opinion. They said "in part of the matter" (*fī baʻḍi al-amr*) as a safeguard for themselves, so that they would not be fully obedient.

As for "those who hated what God had sent down," they are those who hated the Qur'an and disbelieved. They are either:
- The polytheists of Mecca, about whom God, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is because they hated what God had sent down, so He made their deeds fruitless﴾ [Muhammad: 9]. They had ties with the people of Yathrib. When the Prophet ﷺ emigrated to Medina, the Meccans intensified their monitoring of their associates among the people of Yathrib, in order to learn the condition of the Muslims. Perhaps after the Day of Badr they were plotting against the Muslims and preparing to avenge themselves on them, which they accomplished on the Day of Uhud.
- Or the Jews of Qurayza and al-Nadir, about whom God related in His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who practised hypocrisy say to their brethren among the People of the Book who disbelieved?﴾ [al-Hashr: 11].

On the first interpretation, the intended meaning of "part of the matter" in light of His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who turned back on their heels﴾ [Muhammad: 25] is disclosing some of the Muslims' affairs to them and informing them of the large number of hypocrites, even though the hypocrites would not fight because of their aversion to combat.

On the second interpretation, the intended meaning of "part of the matter" is part of the matter of fighting, meaning that scheme they devised for withdrawing from the Muslim army.

"The matter" (*al-amr*) means the affair of polytheism and what suits its adherents. That is, "We will obey you in part of the disbelief, and we will not obey you in all affairs, because that would expose their hypocrisy." Alternatively, the intended meaning is "in part of what you command us," using the verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, as in *al-khalq* ("creation") meaning *al-makhluq* ("the created").

Whichever is the case, they said that to the polytheists in secret. God therefore informed His Prophet ﷺ of it, and for this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and God knows their secrets (*isrārahum*)﴾.

The majority of readers read *asrārahum* with an open hamza, the plural of *sirr* ("secret"). Ḥamza, al-Kisāʼī, and Ḥafṣ from ʻĀṣim, and Khalaf, read it with a hamza kasra, as the verbal noun of *asarra* ("to conceal, to keep secret").
