The fa' (فاء) may be for consequential linking (al-tafrii', التفريع, a connective showing that one statement follows from another) to the clause ﴿Indeed, those who turned back on their heels﴾ [Muhammad: 25] and what follows up to ﴿Satan has made it attractive to them﴾ [Muhammad: 25]. This is based on the first interpretation (al-mahmal al-awwal) of apostasy (al-irtidad). In that case, the consequential link explains what punishment will befall them at death. It is an introduction (istihlal) to what follows of their punishment, from the beginning of death until they settle in the everlasting punishment.

On the second interpretation, that the intended meaning is turning back from fighting, the fa' is eloquent (fasiha, فصيحة, a fa' that indicates an implied condition): it conveys, "If they fled from fighting out of panic and fear, then how will it be when the angels take their souls?" That is, how great will their panic and terror be, the very things by which they turned back from fighting. This requires two things. The first is that they will certainly die. The second is that their death will be accompanied by punishment.

The first is derived by implicit signification (dalalat al-iltizam, دلالة الالتزام, meaning understood by necessary implication), and it is in the sense of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Those who said of their brothers while they sat [at home], "If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed." Say, "Then avert from yourselves death, if you should be truthful"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 168], and His saying, ﴿And they said, "Do not go forth in the heat." Say, "The fire of Hell is more intense in heat, if they only understood"﴾ [al-Tawba: 81].

The second is the explicit meaning of the speech: it is a warning of punishment in this world at the time of death.

The purpose is to warn them that punishment will be hastened upon them from the first stage of the Hereafter, which is the state of death.

Since this punishment is made certain to occur, the interrogation about their state is placed upon it. It is an interrogation used to express the addressee's astonishment at their state at the time of death. This astonishment indicates that it is a dreadful state, unfamiliar, since one is only astonished at something unaccustomed, and the context indicates its dreadfulness.

The adverb (idha, إذا) is connected to an omitted element indicated by the interrogative noun (kayf, كيف). Its estimate is: "What will be their state or their deeds when the angels take them?"

The omission of the complement of (kayf) in such cases, with the estimate placed after (kayf) and (idha), is frequent, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness﴾ [al-Nisa': 41]. The estimate is: "How will they act and contrive?"

Sibawayh (سيبويه) treated kayf in such a construction as an adverb (zarf, ظرف, adverb of time or place), and Ibn al-Hajib (ابن الحاجب) followed him in al-Kafiya (الكافية). Perhaps he intended to avoid the omission.

The clause ﴿striking their faces and their backs﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal, حال) referring to the angels. The purpose of this circumstance is to warn them of this dreadful death which God has decreed for them, and He made the angels strike their faces and their backs. That is, they will strike their faces, which they protected from the blow of the sword when they fled from the struggle (jihad). The faces are indeed what is aimed at with swords in battle. Al-Huraysh al-Qurayi, or al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas, said:

"We expose to the swords, when we meet, faces that are not exposed to the necks (nizam)."

And they strike their backs, which would have been the place of the blow had they fought. This is an allusion (ta'rid, تعريض, indirect implication) that if they had fought, they would have fled, so the blow falls only upon their backs.

This is the commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 28:

﴿That is because they followed what angered God and disliked His good pleasure, so He made their deeds fruitless.﴾

The demonstrative "that" (dhalika) refers to the terrible death that is indicated by His words: ﴿But how will it be when the angels take their souls?﴾ [Muhammad: 27], as was mentioned just before.

Their "following what angered God" is their following of polytheism (shirk).

"Anger" (sukht) is used metaphorically for the absence of approval of an action.

Their "disliking God's good pleasure" means their disliking the means of His good pleasure, which is Islam.

In mentioning "following what angered God" and "disliking His good pleasure" there is the figure of speech tibaq (antithesis), occurring twice, due to the opposition between anger and good pleasure, and between following and disliking.

The combining of the report about them concerning their following of what angered God and their disliking of His good pleasure, although one of them could have sufficed in place of the other, is to indicate that the angels striking their faces is appropriate to their devotion to what angered God, and that their striking their backs is appropriate to their disliking of His good pleasure, because disliking entails turning away and retreating. Thus in the speech there is also the figure of speech called husn al-laff wa al-nashr al-murattab (the ordered wrapping and unfolding).

So that punishment was appropriate to the two states of their attempt to avoid death by fleeing from fighting, and to the two causes that motivated that avoidance.

He then made the statement ﴿so He made their deeds fruitless﴾ as a consequence of their following what angered God and their disliking His good pleasure. Thus their following what angered God and their disliking His good pleasure were the cause of both matters: the angels striking their faces and backs at the time of death, and the nullifying of their deeds.

Ihbat (nullification) is the voiding of an action, meaning that He nullified their benefit from the deeds they had done alongside the believers, such as uttering the word of tawhid, prayer, zakat and other things. What has the same meaning was mentioned at the beginning of the surah.

Page 120

A transition from threat and warning to an admonition that God informs His Messenger ﷺ of what the hypocrites conceal of disbelief, deceit and scheming, so that they know their secrets are not hidden, and thus become certain that they are exhausting their minds in devising plots to no avail, which is a frustration of their hopes.

The particle (am) here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), meaning "bal" (rather) in the sense of a transitional shift (idrab intiqali) from one subject to another. The interrogative implied after (am) is for denial.

The particle (lan) is for the perpetuation of negation (ta'bid al-nafy). That is, they do not suppose that their malice will fail to appear in the future, just as it failed to appear in the past, so perhaps God will expose their hypocrisy.

The word "disease" (maradh) is used metaphorically (istiʿarah, metaphor) for disbelief, based on the common feature of harm to its bearer. Because disbelief has its seat in the intellect, which is expressed by "heart" (qalb), mentioning the hearts alongside the disease serves as a supporting development of the metaphor (tarshih lil-istiʿarah), since the heart is an inner organ and thus suits a hidden disease.

The word "bringing out" (ikhraj) is used for disclosure and manifestation, metaphorically, because bringing out means drawing something from its hiding place. It is thus used in the sense of revealing something hidden.

Al-adghan is the plural of ghin (with a kasrah on the ḍād and sukūn on the ghayn), which means enmity and hatred.

The meaning is that God brings them out of their hearts. The Arabs used to make the hearts the place of rancor. The poet said, and it is among the examples cited in al-Miftah by al-Sakkaki, though his identity is unknown:

"Those who strike every white, keen-edged sword,
and who pierce the very gatherings of rancor."

[Page 121]

﴿Had We willed, We would have shown them to you, and you would have recognized them by their marks.﴾

The sickness in their hearts was hidden, because they went to great lengths to conceal it and disguise it by displaying faith outwardly. So God told His Prophet ﷺ that if He willed, He would have revealed them to him one by one, so that he would know their identities through their marks.

Al-sīmā (with a short vowel on the alif, pronounced *al-sīmā*, meaning "distinguishing mark") means a constant sign. Its original form was *wisma*, on the pattern *fi'lā*, from *al-wasm*, which is placing a mark (*simah*) on a thing. Its first letter takes a kasra. It belongs to the category of verbs with an initial weak letter (*mithāl wāwī*). The wāw was transposed from the position of the first radical to the position of the middle radical, and the middle radical was moved to the position of the first, so it became *siwmā*. The wāw then changed to yā' because it was sukūn and preceded by a kasra. This was discussed earlier, at God's words, ﴿You will recognize them by their marks﴾ (2:273), in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning is: "We would have shown you their persons, and you would have recognized them." Or: "We would have described their attributes to you, and you would have recognized them by these." It is also possible that God willed this and showed them to the Messenger ﷺ. From Anas: "After this verse, nothing of the hypocrites was hidden from the Prophet ﷺ; he knew them by their marks." Al-Baghawi and al-Tha'labi related this without a chain of transmission.

What is reported from Hudhayfah suggests that the Prophet ﷺ was made aware of the hypocrites, or some of them. However, if this report is authentic, God did not command that they be treated differently from the Muslims. It is also possible that God said this as an honour to His Messenger ﷺ, without informing him of them.

The lām in *la-araynākahum* (لأريناكهم) is the lām of the response to *law* (if), which is often added to it.

The lām in *fa-la-ʿarafta-hum* (فلعرفتهم) is an emphatic lām, reinforcing the lām of *la-araynākahum*, to add further confirmation that knowledge follows from the act of showing.

* * *

﴿And you will surely recognize them by the tenor of their speech.﴾

This is said as a safeguard against what the implication of ﴿Had We willed, We would have shown them to you﴾ might suggest, namely that the will to show them by their attributes did not take place.

The meaning is: "If We do not show them to you by their marks, then your knowledge of them will certainly come from the tenor of their speech, through an inspiration God places in the knowledge of His Messenger ﷺ. Nothing of the tenor of their speech will be hidden from him."

Page 122

So he will have knowledge of each one of them whenever he speaks allusively. None of them is free from allusive speech in his talk. Thus the Messenger's knowledge of each one of them is attained. God left aside informing him of them by their marks and entrusted him to know them through the tenor of their speech, preserving the custom of God, exalted is He, in the order of creation as far as is possible, because it is a custom arising from wisdom. When it was desired to honour the Messenger ﷺ by informing him of the hidden matters of the hypocrites, God took the path of allusion in this.

The lām in *wa-la-taʿrifannahum* (ولتعرفنهم) is the lām of the omitted oath.

*Laḥn al-qawl* (لحن القول, "the tenor or allusion of speech") is speech that is turned away from its apparent meaning so that only the one intended to understand it grasps it, and not anyone else. This happens when the speech contains an indirect hint (*taʿrīḍ*), a double meaning (*tawriya*), or terms agreed upon between two persons or a group, like the technical terms of a discipline. Al-Qattal al-Kilā'ī said:

"I have signalled to you so that you may understand,
and I have spoken an allusion that is not doubtful."

The hypocrites used to address the Prophet ﷺ with speech they had agreed upon among themselves, while the Prophet ﷺ took their speech at its outward meaning. God alerted him to this, and after that he would know the hypocrites whenever he heard their speech.

* * *

﴿And God knows your deeds.﴾

This is a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*). Because of its generality, it is addressed to the whole community, and its purpose is instruction. It is also, at the same time, a metonymy (*kināya*) for its necessary implication, which is a warning to the doers of evil deeds regarding their deeds, and a promise to the doers of good deeds regarding their deeds. It is also an admonition to the people of hypocrisy that God is about to expose their hypocrisy, as He said earlier: ﴿Or do those in whose hearts is a sickness think that God will not bring forth their rancour?﴾ (47:29).

The use of the present tense in *yaʿlamu* (يعلم, "knows") indicates that His knowledge of this is continuous.

[Page 123]

﴿And We will surely test you until We know those among you who strive and are steadfast, and We will test your reports.﴾

This is coordinated (*'atf*) with His saying ﴿and Allah knows your deeds﴾ [Muhammad: 30]. Its meaning is a precaution (*ihtiras*, a qualification that guards against a misunderstanding) against what the listeners might suppose from His saying ﴿and Allah knows your deeds﴾, namely that God is thereby independent of imposing obligations (*taklif*).

The rationale for this precaution is that God's knowledge relates to people's deeds after they occur, and it relates to them before they occur, since they will occur. It also relates to people's resolve to respond to the call of the obligations, in strength and in weakness, and to their failure to respond, through disbelief and obstinacy. So this verse makes clear that among the wisdoms of the obligations is that the effect of God's knowledge of people's states should become manifest, and that the proof should be established against them.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, Allah has written for every servant his place, either in Paradise or in the Fire." They said: "Shall we not rely upon what has been written for us?" He said: "Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for." And he recited: ﴿As for he who gives and fears Allah﴾ [al-Layl: 5] ﴿and believes in the best reward﴾ [al-Layl: 6] ﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾ [al-Layl: 7] ﴿But as for he who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-Layl: 8] ﴿and denies the best reward﴾ [al-Layl: 9] ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾ [al-Layl: 10].

*Al-balw* means testing and ascertaining the state of a thing. What is meant by *ibtila'* (trial) here is the command and the prohibition within the obligations, for through them the obedient, the disobedient and the disbelieving become manifest. This was called *ibtila'* by way of *majaz mursal* (metonymy based on a connection, a figurative usage in which a term is applied to a related thing), because trial necessarily accompanies it, even though its primary purpose is to establish the welfare of people and to repel corruption from them, in order to organise the conditions of their lives, and then so that the outcome of eternal life in the Hereafter may follow from it. However, since the obligation clarifies the states of people's souls in compliance, tests their claims and uncovers their inner natures, it came to include what resembles trial. Otherwise, God, exalted is He, knows the details of their states, but these do not become apparent to the eyes of people except upon receiving the obligations, so they resemble testing. Thus applying the name *ibtila'* to the obligation is *majaz mursal*, and calling what necessarily accompanies the obligation, namely the manifestation of the states of souls, a trial is *isti'ara* (metaphor). So in His saying ﴿We will surely test you﴾ there is both *majaz mursal* and *isti'ara*.

*Hatta* (ﷺ) is a particle of termination (*harf intiha'*), so what follows it is the end-point (*ghaya*) of the verb that precedes it. Here it is used with the meaning of the particle of causation *lam al-ta'lil* (the "lam" of purpose), by likening the cause of the act to its end-point, since the end-point of an act generally motivates its doer. For this reason *hatta* is frequently used in the sense of the causal *lam*, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are the ones who say: Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7].

[Page 124]
So the meaning is: "And We will surely test you in order that We may know those among you who strive and are steadfast." It is not meant that the testing ends when the strivers and the steadfast among them become manifest.

The cause of an act does not necessarily entail its converse, that is, it is not necessary that the act have no cause other than this one. Thus the obligations have many causes and purposes, among them that the state of people in accepting the obligations be made manifest in this world, such that worldly dealings are based upon it.

The knowledge of God that is made the cause of the testing is knowledge of things after they occur, called *'ilm al-shahada* (knowledge of the witnessed), because God knows who will strive and who will be steadfast before He tests them. But that is *'ilm al-ghayb* (knowledge of the unseen), since it precedes the realisation of the known in the world of witnessing.

The better view is that *hatta na'lama* (until We know) is used in the sense of *hatta nuzhira* (until We make manifest) to people the true claims from the false. Thus "knowledge" is a metonymic allusion (*kinaya*) to the manifestation of the known thing, regardless of whether its manifestation is to another or to the speaker, as in this verse, or as in the saying of Ias ibn Qabisa al-Ta'i:

*And I advanced while the spear swayed between us, so that I might know which of them is a coward and which a brave man.*

He meant that he might make it manifest to people that he was brave, and that it might become clear who among the people was a coward. God legislated jihad for the support of the religion, and through its legislation it becomes evident who strives and who holds back from jihad, and who is steadfast under the hardships of war and who withdraws and flees. Thus the claim of the hypocrites to sincere faith is not accepted by people, and the believers who were truthful in what they pledged to God become known.

As for the testing of reports, it is the spread of a reputation through good renown or its opposite. This is in the sense of the saying of the jurists of legal theory (*al-Usuliyyun*, scholars of the foundations of jurisprudence): "praise and blame are enacted immediately." It is also an allusion (*kinaya*) to the conditions of their deeds, whether good or evil, because reports are only reports about their deeds. This is a second cause, coordinated (*'uti'at*) with His saying ﴿until We know those among you who strive﴾. The verb *nabluwa* (We test) was repeated in coordination with the verb *na'lama* (We know), whereas the apparent structure would have been to coordinate *akhbarakum* (your reports) with the *waw* onto the pronoun of the addressees in *lanabluwannakum* (We will surely test you), without repeating *nabluwa*. The departure from the apparent structure of the composition to this construction was for the sake of emphasis on the testing of reports, since it is an allusion to the testing of their deeds, which is the purpose of testing their persons. So mentioning it is like mentioning the general after the specific, since the first testing relates to striving and steadfastness, and

[Page 125]
the second testing relates to all deeds. Along with this there occurs verbal emphasis of the testing (*ta'kid lafzi*).

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿lanabluwannakum hatta na'lama﴾ and *nabluwa* with *nun* in all three verbs. Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read these three verbs with the *ya'* of the third person, and the pronouns refer to the Name of Majesty in His saying ﴿and Allah knows your deeds﴾ [Muhammad: 30].

The majority read *wa-nabluwa* with a *fatha* on the *waw*, coordinating it with *na'lama*. Ruways, on the authority of Ya'qub, read it with a *sukun* on the *waw*, coordinating it with *lanabluwannakum*.

[Page 126]

The apparent meaning is that "those who disbelieve" here refers to those who disbelieve mentioned at the beginning of this surah and in the verses that follow, where mention of the disbelievers occurs. That is, the open disbelievers (al-kuffar al-suraha'). The discourse returns to them after finishing the mention of the hypocrites, who conceal disbelief, returning to the starting point (awdan 'ala bad') in order to diminish their status in the hearts of the Muslims. After Allah informed that He had caused their deeds to go astray, that they followed falsehood, and commanded that their necks be struck, and that ruin is theirs, and belittled them by saying that they enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and that Allah destroyed towns that were stronger than them in power, then the mention of the hypocrites occurred. After that, the discourse turns back again to those who disbelieve, so that Allah may inform the Muslims that, in these critical situations between them and the polytheists, no harm of any kind will reach them from them, and in order to increase the description of those who disbelieve by stating that they opposed the Messenger ﷺ.

So the sentence is a fresh resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i, a new independent sentence), and it is a preparatory introduction (tawti'ah) to His saying: ﴿So do not weaken and call to peace﴾ [Muhammad: 35].

The verb "shaqqu" (شاقوا) is derived from the word shiqq (شِقّ), with a kasra on the shin, meaning side. Al-mushaqqah (المشاقّة) means opposition. Opposition is expressed by this word metaphorically (kunniya), because one who stands on one side opposes one who stands on another side, and so both are opposed to each other. For this reason the form mufa'alah (مفاعلة) is derived from it.

The manifestation of guidance to them (tabayyun al-huda lahum) means the appearance of the truth in the call of Islam, which the intellects grasp when they are alerted to it, and the appearance that the affair of Islam is increasing and growing, while the affairs of others are in decline. Yet this did not deter them from attempting to harm the Messenger ﷺ, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41].

From the totality of this it results that the Messenger ﷺ is the Messenger of Allah, and that Islam is the religion of Allah.

It has also been said that what is meant by "those who disbelieve" in this verse is the Jews of Qurayza and al-Nadir. In that case their opposition to the Messenger ﷺ is a hidden opposition, the opposition of cunning and deceit. And the manifestation of guidance to them is the appearance that Muhammad ﷺ is the one promised in the Torah and the books of the prophets. Thus the verse would be a preparation for the campaigns against Qurayza and al-Nadir.

"Shay'an" (شيئًا) is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq, a cognate object) of "yadurru" (يضرّوا), and the tanwin is for diminution, meaning they will not harm Allah in the future even the least harm.

The harm to Allah is intended to mean the harm to His religion, for the purpose of honouring and ennobling this religion, as indicated by His saying: ﴿and opposed the Messenger after guidance had become clear to them﴾.

Al-ihbat (الإحباط) is nullification, as has been mentioned just before.

The meaning of nullifying their deeds, in relation to their deeds in dealing with the Muslims, is that Allah shows kindness to His Messenger ﷺ and the Muslims by facilitating the means of their victory and the spread of His religion, so the disbelievers do not obtain any worthwhile result from their deeds of hindering and opposing. This is as was mentioned earlier in the explanation of His saying: "He has caused their deeds to go astray."

The future particle here (harf al-istiqbal, the particle of the future) is for affirming that the nullification will occur in the future. It indicates that Allah is nullifying their deeds from now on, since that is not beyond His power, so that He would wait for the future to bring it about. This affirmation is like what is in His saying in Surah Yusuf: ﴿He said, "I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you."﴾ [Yusuf: 98].

[p. 127]

This is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) placed between the sentence ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah and oppose the Messenger﴾ [Muhammad: 32] and the sentence ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah, then die while they are disbelievers﴾ [Muhammad: 34]. It is directed at the believers, commanding them to obey Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and to avoid what nullifies righteous deeds, by way of taking a lesson from what has been related of the state of the polytheists in barring [others] from the way of Allah and opposing the Messenger ﷺ.

So the description of faith in His words ﴿O you who believe﴾ stands in contrast to the description of disbelief in His words ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ [Muhammad: 32]. Obedience to Allah is the opposite of barring from the way of Allah, obedience to the Messenger is the opposite of opposing the Messenger ﷺ, and the prohibition against nullifying deeds is the opposite of the nullification of the deeds of those who disbelieved.

The obedience to the Messenger ﷺ that they were commanded to observe is complying with what he commanded and prohibited of the rulings of the religion. As for matters that do not fall under legislation (tashri'), obedience to his command in them is obedience of sincere counsel and good manners. Do you not see that Barira did not obey the Messenger of Allah ﷺ regarding returning to her husband Mughith, when she knew that his command to her was not a binding resolve?

Ibtal (nullification, from the root b-ṭ-l) means making a thing void, that is, rendering it without benefit. Thus, it is things that exist that are described as being nullified.

The meaning of the prohibition against their nullifying deeds is the prohibition against the causes of their nullification. This is the evident sense of His words ﴿and do not nullify your deeds﴾. Its possible meanings permit it to include the prohibition and warning against everything that the religion has explained as nullifying an act, wholly or partly, such as apostasy, and such as showing off (riya') in a righteous deed, for it nullifies its reward. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that [Allah] the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders [of your giving] and injury﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264]. Some of the early generations (salaf) feared that committing indecencies (fawahish) nullifies the reward of righteous deeds, and they took this verse to mean that. 'A'isha said, when she learned that Zayd ibn Arqam had concluded a contract which 'A'isha regarded as unlawful: "Inform Zayd that he has nullified his jihad with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ unless he abandons this act of his." It may be that she intended this as a warning; otherwise, what is the point of specifying the nullification of his jihad? She only knew that it was the most precious deed to him.

It is also related from al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Zuhri: "Do not nullify your deeds with the major sins (al-kaba'ir)."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr mentioned in al-Isti'ab that Zayd ibn Arqam said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ fought nineteen battles, and I fought seventeen of them alongside him."

All of these are among the differing understandings concerning what is meant by the nullification of deeds and what nullifies them. The best of the sayings of the early generations on this is what is related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "We used to think that none of our good deeds was unaccepted, until there was revealed ﴿and do not nullify your deeds﴾. So we said: 'What is this that nullifies our deeds?' We said: 'The grave sins that necessitate [punishment] and the indecencies.' Then there was revealed ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. So we refrained from speculation on that. We used to fear for those who committed grave sins and hope for those who did not commit them." Thus he made clear that these are possible interpretations, with no certainty in them.

It is also related from Muqatil concerning ﴿do not nullify your deeds with reminders [of your giving]﴾, and he said: "This is an address to a people of the Banu Asad who had embraced Islam and said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'We have preferred you, and we have come to you with our souls and our families,' thereby counting it as a favour upon him. So this verse was revealed concerning them, and there was also revealed concerning them His words, the Exalted: ﴿They count it as a favour to you that they have embraced Islam. Say: Do not count your Islam as a favour to me﴾ [al-Hujurat: 17]."

These interpretations arise from opinion and conjecture. What the Qur'an has brought, and what the sound Sunnah has explained, is that good deeds remove evil deeds, and it has not come that evil deeds remove good deeds. He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [anyone] by an atom's weight; and if it is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward﴾ [al-Nisa': 40].

The Mu'tazila (a rationalist school) adhered to this verse and claimed that grave sins nullify acts of obedience.

It is strange that they deny injustice (zulm) to Allah, yet do not accept the apparent sense of His words ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23], and yet they make Allah nullify good deeds when their doer commits an evil deed.

We hold that all of this is inscribed in the records of good and evil deeds, and that a good deed is multiplied while an evil deed is [recorded] according to its measure. This is a principle whose meaning has been transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur) in the Book and in authentic reports. So how can it be rejected on the basis of the talk and gossip of some people of reports?

Some of our scholars interpreted His words, the Exalted, ﴿and do not nullify your deeds﴾ as meaning a prohibition against breaking off a deed through which one draws near to Allah, the Exalted. Applying the term nullification to breaking off and failing to complete [an act] seems to be a metaphor (majaz); that is, do not abandon a righteous deed after beginning it. From this they derived that a voluntary act (nafl) becomes obligatory upon commencement, since it is among the deeds. This is the view of Abu Hanifa regarding supererogatory acts in general. Ibn al-'Arabi in al-Ahkam attributed a similar view to Malik, and so did al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Furs. [p. 129] The Shaykh al-Jadd, in his marginal notes on al-Mahalli, transmitted from al-Qarafi in his commentary on al-Mahsul, and Hallulu, in his commentary on Jam' al-Jawami', transmitted from al-Qarafi in al-Dhakhira, that Malik held that seven voluntary acts become obligatory upon commencement, namely: prayer, fasting, the Hajj, the 'Umrah, i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque), the congregational following of an imam (i'timam), and voluntary circumambulation (tawaf al-tatawwu'), and no others, such as ablution (wudu'), charity, endowment (waqf), or travel for jihad. Hallulu added the sacrifice (al-dahiyya) to the voluntary acts that become obligatory upon commencement. I have not found the basis of al-Qarafi's position on this, nor the basis of Hallulu's addition in the latter case.

Al-Shafi'i did not hold that any voluntary act becomes obligatory upon commencement, and this is the apparent view.

This verse completes the verse ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah and oppose the Messenger﴾ [Muhammad: 32] and so on, because that verse was brought to indicate disregard for their opposition and to show that Allah nullifies their deeds. This verse, however, is brought to show that they will not benefit from Allah's forgiveness, since they died upon the disbelief they were in. Therefore it is a new sentence, a resumptive beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i).

The linking of the predicate of the relative clause with the particle "fa" (fa') is an indication that it carries the meaning of the conditional (shart). So it does not refer to a specific individual of the relative clause; rather, it refers to everyone in whom the essence of the relative clause is realized, namely disbelief and dying upon disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 35:

﴿So do not weaken and call to peace, while you are the superior ones, and Allah is with you, and He will not deprive you of your deeds.﴾

The fa' (فَ) here indicates a consequence (lil-tafri') of what had been established in the souls of the believers: that Allah, exalted is He, forsook the polytheists, by what He had informed of, that He had caused their deeds to go astray and decreed ruin for them, and by the examples He had set forth of the fates of their likes among those before them, whom Allah destroyed and annihilated, and who found no helper; and by what He had promised the believers of victory over them, and what He had commanded them of fighting them, and by His undertaking to be the protector of the believers, and by what He had promised them of reward in the abode of eternity, and by what followed that of description of the scheming of the faction of the hypocrites against the believers

Page 130
and their pledge to aid the polytheists. This is something the believers fear, since they know that enemies of theirs are scattered among them.

Upon all of that He made consequent His prohibition to them from weakness and from inclining towards ease, and His promise to them that they are the victorious ones and that Allah supports them.

It is also permissible that the fa' be taken as consequent upon the nearest of the preceding reports, which is His saying: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those of you who strive and the patient﴾ [Muhammad: 31].

This prohibition against weakness and against calling to peace is a warning against a matter whose causes of occurrence were abundant, being ready to advance into war when commanded to it. It is not a prohibition against a weakness that had already occurred among them, nor against their calling to peace, because this surah was revealed after the Battle of Badr and before the Battle of Uhud, during a period in which there was no fighting between the Muslims and the polytheists. Rather, the warning is against the hypocrites causing them to become feeble when the matter of fighting is directed, so that they say: "If only we had made peace with the people for a period until we restore our equipment and regain our strength after the Day of Badr." Abu Sufyan and those with him among the polytheists, when they returned to Makkah defeated after the encounter of Badr, were watching for an opportunity to fight the Muslims, because of what troubled them of the Muslims' intercepting them on the route of their trade to Syria, as occurred in the Battle of al-Sawiq and the Battle of Dhi Qarad. When there were hypocrites in Madinah, and there were men of the people of Yathrib with the people of Makkah who had left it with Abu 'Amir al-Dubai, who was known in the Jahiliyyah as al-Rahib (the monk), and whose title the Prophet ﷺ changed, calling him al-Fasiq (the depraved one).

It was to be expected that their enemies among the people of Yathrib would scheme against the Muslims, aiding the polytheists against them while concealing themselves behind the pretext of seeking peace. So Allah warned them against falling into this snare.

Al-wahn (الوَهَنُ): weakness and incapacity. Here it is a metaphor for seeking ease. Its meaning: the prohibition against surrendering their selves to thoughts of weakness. Acting upon this prohibition is by bringing to mind the evils of those thoughts, for evil thoughts, if a person's resolve does not resist them, creep into his soul little by little until they take hold of him and become a disposition and a character trait. The meaning is: repel from your selves the thoughts of weakness and avoid its manifestations, the first of which is calling to peace, which is the intended object of the prohibition.

The prohibition against weakness implies that they were not, on that day, in a state of weakness.

Page 131
The conjunction of "wa tad'ū" (وتَدْعُوا) with "tahinū" (تَهِنُوا) makes it governed by the particle of prohibition, and the meaning is: "and do not call to peace." This is a specific conjunction over a general one in one respect, because calling to peace while able is a seeking of ease without benefit. It was singled out for mention lest it be thought that there is in it the benefit of preserving lives and the gain of rest from the enemy's assault upon the Muslims, since the polytheists at that time were pressing upon the Muslims. Perhaps the Muslims would think that if they called to peace together with them they would be safe from them, and would take that as an opportunity to spread the call. So Allah made known to them that this would return to them with harm, because it would lower their standing in the eyes of the polytheists, who would reckon that they sought peace out of weakness, which would increase their aggression against them, and the tribes of the Arabs would look lightly upon them after they had held in their hearts a place of reverence and anticipation of their might.

For this subtle purpose, the prohibition against weakness and the calling to peace were combined, and it was followed by His saying: ﴿while you are the superior ones﴾.

What is established from what has been stated is that the calling to peace that is forbidden is the seeking of a settlement from the enemy while the Muslims are capable and the enemy fears them. It is thus peace restricted by the condition that the Muslims are the ones calling to it, and that it is from weakness while in a state of strength. Qatadah said: that is, do not be the first of the two groups to humble itself to its counterpart. This does not contradict the peace permitted in His saying: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [al-Anfal: 61] in Surah al-Anfal, for that is peace sought by the enemy. So this verse does not abrogate the verse of al-Anfal, nor the reverse, and each has its particular situation. It is also restricted by the condition that the Muslims are in a state of strength, might and numbers, such that they call to peace out of desire for ease.

So if the Muslims have an interest in peace, or if it is less harmful to them, then they may initiate it when they need it, and they may respond to it when it is called to them.

The Prophet ﷺ made peace with the polytheists on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah for a benefit that became apparent afterwards. The Muslims, in their campaign to Ifriqiyya, made peace with its people and withdrew returning to Egypt. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said in a statement to one of the army commanders: "I have preferred the safety of the Muslims." As for a settlement over part of the land together with its conquest, that does not contradict the strength of the conquerors, just as the commanders of Abu Bakr made peace with half the people of Damascus, and as the commanders of 'Umar made peace with the people of the fertile land of Iraq, and they were more knowledgeable about what was good for them.

Page 132
The majority read "ilā al-silm" (إلى السَّلْمِ) with a fatha on the sin. Abu Bakr, from 'Asim and Hamzah, read it with a kasra on the sin, and both are dialects.

The clause ﴿while you are the superior ones﴾ is conjoined to the prohibition as a conjunction of a declarative sentence to an imperative, and the declarative is used in the sense of a promise.

Al-a'lawna (الأعْلَوْنَ): an intensive form of loftiness. Here it means dominance and victory, as in His saying to Musa: ﴿Indeed, you are the superior one﴾ [Ta-Ha: 68], that is, Allah is making you victorious.

"And Allah is with you" is conjoined to the promise. The "ma'iyyah" (مَعِيَّةُ) is the ma'iyyah of protection and guardianship, that is, Allah is your guardian and protector, so He will not give the disbelievers any way over you. The meaning: you are the victors by the care and support of Allah.

Each of the two clauses ﴿you are the superior ones﴾ and ﴿Allah is with you﴾ is phrased as a nominal sentence to indicate the permanence of victory for them and the permanence of Allah's care for them.

His saying ﴿and He will not deprive you of your deeds﴾ is a promise of the firmness of their deeds and their success, the opposite of His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of Allah, He has caused their deeds to go astray﴾ [Muhammad: 1]. So the success and prosperity of deeds is expressed by their not being diminished, that is, not being reduced, since it is known that if He does not diminish them, then it is more fitting that He not nullify them, that is, not frustrate them. This is what was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And those who fought in the way of Allah, He will never let their deeds go astray. He will guide them and set right their condition﴾ [Muhammad: 4].

It is said: wataraho yatiruhu watran and wittatan (وَتَرَهُ يَتِرَهُ وَتْرًا وَتِرَةً), like wa'ada, when he diminished it. In the hadith of the Muwatta': "Whoever misses the 'Asr prayer, it is as if he has been deprived (wutira) of his family and his wealth."

It is also permissible that it means its literal sense: that He will diminish your reward for your deeds, that is, the jihad which is implied by His saying: ﴿So do not weaken and call to peace﴾, and thus it conveys exhortation to jihad with the promise of its full reward.

This is a reason for what is stated in His words ﴿So do not weaken and call for peace﴾ [Muhammad: 35], and beginning it with (inna) (indeed) makes unnecessary beginning it with the causal fa' (so), as he explained in Dala'il al-I'jaz (Dalā'il al-I'jāz). The attachment of (inna) to the superfluous, restrictive (ma) (mā) does not change its position without (ma), because its attachment to it added the meaning of restriction.

[Page 133]

What is meant by "the life" is the conditions of the duration of life, so it is by omitting two modifiers.

And play (la'ib) is an action whose doer intends by it jest, without gaining any benefit, like the actions of children in their frolicking.

And diversion (lahw) is an action performed to divert the mind from the fatigue of earnestness in matters, so one diverts himself from what concerns him and wearies his mind.

The statement about life that it is play and diversion is in the sense of an eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh). The conditions of the present life are likened to play and diversion in that no benefit results from them, because they are transient and come to an end, while the Hereafter is the abode of permanence.

And this is a warning against letting the love of the delights of living lead them to renounce confronting the enemy and to incline toward reconciling with him, for that would embolden the enemy against them.

The love of a youth for a long life humiliates him, even if he has in him pride and resolve.

[Page 134]

It is most likely that this is coordinated with His saying, ﴿So do not weaken and call to peace﴾ [Muhammad: 35], as a reminder that complying with this prohibition is the praiseworthy *taqwa* (God-consciousness). Calling to peace may be motivated by a love of keeping the wealth that would otherwise be spent on the raid. So they are reminded here of faith and *taqwa*, so that they may strip the weakness from themselves, since they were forbidden from it and from calling to peace. Refraining from that is therefore a form of *taqwa*. Coordinated with this is the statement that God does not ask them for their wealth except for their own benefit and the reform of their affairs. For this reason, after it comes His saying, ﴿Here you are, those who are called to spend in the way of God﴾ [Muhammad: 38], up to His saying "from himself." The position of this sentence is to give the reason for the earlier prohibition, stated in His saying, ﴿The life of this world is only play and amusement﴾ [Muhammad: 36], indicating that when the life of this world is made prosperous with faith and *taqwa*, it becomes a cause of lasting good.

[Page 134 continues]

The *ujur* (rewards) here are the rewards of the Hereafter, which are the reward of faith and *taqwa*.
So the address is to the Muslims addressed in His saying, "So do not weaken," and so on.

The purpose of the sentence is His saying, "and you fear God" (*wa tattaqu*). As for the mention of "you believe" (*tu'minu*), it is for the emphasis on the matter of faith. The placement of *tu'minu* within the conditional clause, even though their faith is already established, determines that the meaning of the conditional here is the intention of continuing in faith, since the reality of *taqwa* is not established except with faith preceding it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Freeing a neck, or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ [Al-Balad: 13], up to His saying, ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾ [Al-Balad: 17], and so on.

It is apparent that the clause ﴿He will give you your rewards﴾ [Muhammad: 36] is an *idmaj* (an insertion within the flow of discourse), and that the intended meaning of the answer to the condition is the clause ﴿and He will not ask you for your wealth﴾ [Muhammad: 36].

The coordination of ﴿and He will not ask you for your wealth﴾ [Muhammad: 36] is for the sake of its connection to His saying, ﴿He will give you your rewards﴾ [Muhammad: 36]. That is, God bestows His favours upon you and does not need your wealth. These connections are the best links for arranging the intended meaning of these admonitions, because stinginess with wealth is one of the motives for calling to peace, as you have learned just now.

The meaning of the verse is: "If you believe and fear God by following what you have been forbidden, God will be pleased with you for that and will be content with it, and He will not ask you for more of your wealth." It is thereby known that what the Prophet (ﷺ) requires of them in spending in the way of God is only according to their capacity.

A parallel to this verse concerning spending is His saying, exalted is He, addressed to a group of Muslims regarding going out to *jihad* (struggle in the way of God): ﴿O you who believe, what is wrong with you that when you are told to march forth in the way of God, you cling heavily to the earth? Are you pleased with the life of this world rather than the Hereafter? The enjoyment of the life of this world, compared with the Hereafter, is but little﴾ [At-Tawbah: 38], in the Surah "Bara'ah" (At-Tawbah).

So His saying, ﴿and He will not ask you for your wealth﴾ [Muhammad: 36], by its generality and its context, conveys the meaning: He does not ask you for all of your wealth. That is, He asks you only for what does not burden you. The addition of *amwal* (wealth), which is a plural, to the pronoun of the addressees conveys generality, so what is negated is the request to spend all of the wealth. Thus the statement is a negation of generality, not a generality of negation, by the indication of the context, and what comes after it is His saying, ﴿Here you are, those who are called to spend in the way of God﴾ [Muhammad: 38], and so on.

[Page 135]

It is also permissible that it conveys the meaning that He does not demand from you the giving of wealth for its own sake, since He is independent of you, and He only commands you to spend wealth for your own good, as He said: ﴿Whoever is stingy, is stingy only against himself. God is the Self-Sufficient, and you are the needy﴾ [Muhammad: 38].
This is a preparation for His saying after it: ﴿Here you are, those who are called to spend in the way of God﴾ [Muhammad: 38], up to His saying, ﴿is stingy only against himself﴾ [Muhammad: 38]. That is, the request to give up wealth is only for the benefit of the community. And what benefit is greater than repelling the enemy from it, so that he does not corrupt it and enslave it?

As for interpreting the negated request for wealth as a demand for the *zakat* (obligatory almsgiving) on wealth, this is a diversion of the verse from its clear course, since *zakat* was obligatory before the revelation of this Surah, for *zakat* was enjoined in the second year after the *Hijrah* (migration), according to the most correct view.

The clause ﴿If He asks you for it﴾ and so on is an explanation for the negation of His asking them for their wealth. That is: because if He asked you to give all of your wealth, while He knows that among you are those who are generous with wealth, you would not be stingy in giving, but you would make the imposition of it a cause for revealing your resentment towards those who do not give. Then apostasy and hypocrisy would increase, and that contradicts God's intent of purifying the souls of those who enter into faith.

This is a consideration of the state of many people at that time in Medina, who were recent converts to Islam, and who had given some of their wealth to the emigrants (*muhajirun*). So God made it easy for them by not asking them for more than that. Among them were many of the hypocrites (*munafiqun*) who watched for opportunities to tempt them. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God until they disperse"﴾ [Al-Munafiqun: 7]. This is indicated by the coordination of His saying, ﴿and He will bring out your resentments﴾. That is: resentments arise among you, so His asking for your wealth becomes a cause of their manifestation, as if He had brought them out. This verse is a foundation for blocking the means to corruption (*sadd al-dhara'i'*).

*Al-Ihfa'* (the insistence): it means increasing and reaching the limit in an action. One says, "He insisted (*ahfahu*) in the request" when he leaves nothing of insistence. It is reported from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd: "*Al-ihfa'* is that you take everything with both your hands," and this is a strange interpretation. It is used here to express the firmness in the request, which is obligation. That is: He obliges you to give wealth and makes a penalty upon withholding it.

*Al-bukhl* (stinginess): withholding the giving of wealth.

[Page 136]

*Al-dighn* (resentment): enmity. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿that God will not bring forth their resentments﴾ [Muhammad: 29].
The meaning is: they withhold the wealth and show disobedience and dislike. So God's gentleness towards many of them required that He not ask them for wealth in the manner of obligation. Then this gradually changed when faith settled in their hearts, and God then made spending in *jihad* obligatory upon them.

The hidden pronoun in *wa yukhrij* (and He will bring out) refers to the name of God (Allah). It is also permissible that it refers to stinginess (*bukhl*), understood from His saying, "you are stingy" (*tabkhulu*), that is, of the kind of His saying, ﴿Be just, that is nearer to *taqwa*﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 8].

The majority (*Jumhur*) of readers recited *yukhrij* with a *ya'* (y) at its beginning. Ya'qub recited it with a *nun* (n) at its beginning.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 38 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Here you are, you who are called upon to spend in the way of God, yet among you are those who are miserly. Whoever is miserly is only miserly against himself. God is the Rich, and you are the poor.﴾

The statements of the exegetes from His words ﴿And He will not ask you for your wealth﴾ [Muhammad: 36] up to His words "against himself" indicate their bewilderment about what God intends by this speech. We have already explained it sufficiently, but there remains His words ﴿Here you are, you who are called upon to spend﴾ and so on: how does it fit after His words ﴿And He will not ask you for your wealth﴾ [Muhammad: 36]? For the call to spend is itself a request for wealth. So how can what is said here be reconciled with His words just mentioned, ﴿And He will not ask you for your wealth﴾ [Muhammad: 36]?

It is possible that the meaning is: you are called to spend in the way of God in order to ward off your enemies from yourselves, and not so that God benefits from it, as He said: ﴿God is the Rich, and you are the poor.﴾

The structure of the speech requires that this be a call to spending in the present, not an announcement to them that they will be called to spend, which would be a request already fulfilled. The word "you are called" (tud'awna) is understood to mean "you are commanded" (tu'marun), i.e., a command of obligation.

It is also possible that "you are called" (tud'awna) be understood as a call of encouragement, so that the verse serves as a preparation for the verses that impose the obligation of spending in the future, like His verse ﴿And strive with your wealth and your selves in the way of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 41] and similar ones. It is also possible that it is an announcement that they will be called to spend in the way of God after this time, so that the imperfect verb is used for the future tense, and the imperfect verb in its original form allows for this.

[p. 137]

On both possibilities, His words ﴿among you are those who are miserly. Whoever is miserly is only miserly against himself﴾ are either delivered in the manner of rebuke, or in the manner of drawing attention to the error of stinginess in giving wealth to jihad, which is the subject of the context; for a person may be miserly in a way whose miserliness does not return to harm himself.

The meaning of His words ﴿is only miserly against himself﴾ on the first possibility is: he is only miserly against himself, since his enemy becomes able to dominate him, so his miserliness returns as harm upon him. On the second possibility, he is only miserly against himself by depriving it of the reward of spending.

The restriction (qasr) conveyed by "innama" (only) is a restriction by reversal (qasr qalb), with respect to the necessary consequence of his miserliness, because the miser believes that he has withheld from the one who called him to spend, but the necessary consequence of his miserliness returns upon him by depriving himself of the benefits of that spending. Thus the restriction is a comprehensive metonymy (majaz mursal murakkab). The verb "bakhila" (to be miserly) takes "'an" (from) because it implies withholding, and it takes "'ala" (against) because it implies restricting the one who is deprived. Here it is followed by the particle "'an."

"Ha antum ha'ula'i" (Here you are) is composed of the particle "ha" (an interjection of alerting) at the beginning of the sentence, the pronoun of address, and then the interjection "ha" that enters upon the demonstrative noun, which serves to emphasise the meaning of the pronoun. Its parallel is His words ﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf in the life of this world﴾ [al-Nisa': 109] in surah al-Nisa'. The more common usage is that the demonstrative in such a construction is without "ha," relying on the interjection "ha" at the beginning of the composition, as in His words, may He be exalted, ﴿Here you are, you love them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119] in surah Al 'Imran.

The clause "you are called" (tud'awna) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the demonstrative, and the whole of this indicates that the meaning of the circumstantial clause is clearly established for its subject.

Many grammarians claimed that omitting the demonstrative after "ha ana" (here I am) and similar constructions is ungrammatical, because the entry of the alerting "ha" upon a noun other than a demonstrative has not been heard, as mentioned by the author of Mughni al-Labib, based on the view that the alerting "ha" mentioned at the beginning of the speech is the one that enters upon demonstratives in such words as "hadha" and "ha'ula'i," and that the pronoun mentioned after it separates it from the demonstrative. However, this occurs in the speech of the author of al-Mughni in the preface of his book, when he said: "Wa ha ana ba'ihun bima asrartuhu" (Here I am, revealing what I had concealed), and in two other places of it, which Badr al-Din al-Damamini pointed out in his commentary "al-Mazj 'ala al-Mughni", and he mentioned in his commentary, known as "al-Hawashi al-Hindiyya", that al-Zamakhshari's example in al-Mufassal, "laha inna Zaydan munṭaliqun" (to her, indeed Zayd is leaving), implies the permissibility of "ha ana af'alu" (here I do), but al-Radi said: "I have not found evidence for the occurrence of that."

The clause ﴿God is the Rich, and you are the poor﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for what precedes it. God is the Rich absolutely, and the absolutely Rich does not ask people for wealth in any matter, and those addressed are poor, so generosity cannot be expected from them. It is thus established that their being called to spend in the way of God is a call to dispose of their wealth for their own benefits, as His words ﴿and whoever is miserly is only miserly against himself﴾ indicate.

The definite article in "al-Ghaniyy" (the Rich) and in "al-Fuqara'" (the poor) is the definite article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), and in both it indicates the perfection of the genus in what is predicated of it. Since they occur as two predicates, both definite, they convey restriction (hasr), that is, the restriction of the attribute to the one qualified: the restriction of the genus of richness to God, and the restriction of the genus of poverty to those addressed by "antum" (you). This is a restriction by claim (qasr idda'i) in both cases, grounded in the signification of "al" as indicating the perfection of the genus. The perfection of richness belongs to God without doubt, given its comprehensiveness and permanence, even if richness may be attributed in part to others. As for the perfection of poverty among people, it is in relation to God's richness, even if they may become rich in some circumstances, but that richness is small and not lasting.

﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, and they will not be like you﴾ is a conjunction (ataf) upon His words ﴿And if you believe and fear God, He will give you your rewards﴾ [Muhammad: 36].

"Al-tawalli" means turning back, and it is used here metaphorically for exchanging faith for disbelief. That is why its recompense is made to be the replacement of them by another people, just as they exchanged the religion of God for the religion of polytheism.

"Al-istibdal" means substitution (tabdil). The "sin" and "ta'" are for intensification. Its object is "qawman" (a people). The thing substituted with is omitted, and what indicates its implied term is His word "ghayrakum" (other than you). It is known that what is substituted with is what "ghayr" is attached to, since the substitution is restricted to two things, so when one of them is mentioned the other is understood.

The implied meaning is: He will substitute a people in place of you, because what is customarily used with the verbs of substitution and exchange is that the object is the one replaced, and what follows "bi" (with) is the replacement, as in His words ﴿Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61], which was discussed in surah al-Baqarah. Though both complements are, in meaning, replaced and replacing according to differing viewpoints, that is why in this verse the complement with "bi" is omitted alongside the object, for brevity.

The meaning is: He will take a people other than you for faith and piety. This does not imply that God will not bring about other peoples except when those addressed apostatise. Rather, the intention is: if you apostatise from the religion, there will be for God a people among the believers who will not apostatise, and there will be for God a people who enter faith and do not apostatise.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of God recited this verse ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, and they will not be like you﴾. They said: 'And who will be substituted for us?' So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) struck the shoulder of Salman al-Farisi, then said: 'This one and his people; this one and his people.'" Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith (a hadith with a single narrator at some stage of the chain). Its chain has some criticism."

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated this hadith on the condition of Muslim, and added in it: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, if faith were suspended from the Pleiades, men from Persia would reach it."

I say: it indicates that the Persians, if they believe, do not apostatise, and it is among the proofs of the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), for some of the Arab tribes apostatised after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Berbers apostatised twelve times after the conquest of their lands and their faith, as related by Shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn Abi Zayd. The people of Persia did not apostatise after their faith.

The "thumma" (then) here indicates rank-based sequence (tartib rutbi), to convey the importance of the quality of steadfastness in faith and its superiority over mere faith, that is: "and they will not be like you in turning away."

The clause is conjoined by "thumma" to the clause ﴿He will substitute a people other than you﴾, so it lies within the domain of the answer to the conditional. A verb conjoined to the answer of the conditional by a conjunctive particle may be jussive (jazm) by coordination, or nominative (raf') by resumption (isti'naf). It has come in this verse in the jussive, and in His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you, and then they will not be helped﴾ [Al 'Imran: 111], in the nominative. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) offered a reason for preferring the jussive here and the resumption there. He said: "Although it is permissible, there is a subtle point, which is that here it cannot be connected to the turning away, because if they do not turn away they will be among those whom God brings in obedience, and if they turn away they will not be like them, because they are disobedient, and those whom God brings are obedient. As for there, whether they fight or do not fight, they will not be helped, so there was no conditional connection there, that is, to the condition, so it was made nominative by the inceptive (ibtida'), while here it was made jussive for the conditional connection." End of quote. It is subtle, and it may be added that the verb conjoined to the answer in the verse of Al 'Imran falls at the end of the verse-ending (fasila), whose sisters all rhyme on the letters waw and nun. So if the jussive of the verb were preferred, the nun would be removed and the verse-ending would be disrupted.

**Surah al-Fath**

The surah beginning ﴿Indeed We have granted you a clear victory﴾ [al-Fath: 1] was called (Surat al-Fath) in the speech of the Companions. In Sahih al-Bukhari it is related from 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal, with a marked ghayn, an open fa and a shadda, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) recited Surat al-Fath on the day of the conquest of Mecca, and he repeated it in it." In it is the hadith of Sahl ibn Hunayf: "We indeed saw ourselves at al-Hudaybiyya, and if you had seen fighting, we would have fought." Then he (al-Bukhari) related the statement of 'Umar, until he said: "Then Surat al-Fath was revealed," and no other name for it is known.

The reason for the name is that it included the account of the conquest of God's decision for His Prophet (ﷺ), as will come.

It is a Medinan surah according to the well-known terminology, that what was revealed after the Hijra is Medinan, even if its revelation was in a place other than Medina, whether in its territory or elsewhere. This surah was revealed at a place called Kura' al-Ghamim, with a damma on the kaf in Kura' and a fatha on the marked ghayn and a kasra on the mim in al-Ghamim, a place between Mecca and Medina. It is a valley two stages from Mecca and three miles from 'Usfan, and it is in the land of Mecca. It was said it was revealed at Dajnan, on the pattern of Sakran, which is a mountain near Mecca. It was revealed at night, so it is among the nocturnal Qur'an.

Its revelation was in the sixth year after the Hijra, on the Prophet's (ﷺ) return from al-Hudaybiyya and before the expedition of Khaybar. In the Muwatta' it is related from 'Umar: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was travelling on some of his journeys, that is, on his return from al-Hudaybiyya, at night, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab was travelling with him. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab asked him about something, but he did not answer him. Then he asked him again, and he did not answer him. Then he asked him again, and he did not answer him. So 'Umar said: 'May the mother of 'Umar be bereaved! You pressed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) three times, and each time he does not answer you.' 'Umar said: 'So I urged my camel on and went ahead of the people, and I feared that a Qur'an might be revealed concerning me. Not long after, I heard a crier calling out to me. I said: "Indeed I feared that a Qur'an had been revealed concerning me." So I came to the Messenger of God and greeted him, and he said: "Indeed a surah has been revealed to me tonight, which is dearer to me than what the sun rises upon." Then he recited: ﴿Indeed We have granted you a clear victory﴾ [al-Fath: 1].'" The meaning of his words "it is dearer to me than what the sun rises upon" is because of what it includes of His words ﴿That God may forgive you your earlier and later sins﴾ [al-Fath: 2].

Muslim and al-Tirmidhi related from Anas, who said: "There was revealed to the Prophet ﴿That God may forgive you your earlier and later sins﴾ [al-Fath: 2], up to His words ﴿a great victory﴾, on his return from al-Hudaybiyya. So the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed a verse has been revealed to me which is dearer to me than everything upon the face of the earth.' Then he recited it."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 47, verse 38 (part 2 of 2):**

It is the 113th surah in the order of revelation according to the view of Jabir ibn Zayd. It was revealed after Surat al-Saff and before Surat al-Tawba.

The number of its verses is twenty-nine.

The occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is what al-Wahidi and Ibn Ishaq narrated from al-Miswar ibn Makhrama and Marwan ibn al-Hakam, who said: "Surat al-Fath was revealed between Makkah and Madinah concerning the affair of al-Hudaybiyya, when we had been prevented from performing our rites, so we were in grief and sorrow. Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾ [al-Fath: 1]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There has been revealed to me a verse that is dearer to me than the world and everything in it.'" There is also a narration of it from beginning to end.

**Its purposes:**

This surah contains the good tidings to the believers that the outcome of the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya is good, and that it is a victory and an opening (fath). Through it, tranquility (sakina) descended into the hearts of the Muslims, and it removed their grief over being barred from visiting the House for the 'umra (lesser pilgrimage). The Muslims were a number that could not be defeated despite their small size, yet they saw that they had returned like the disappointed. So Allah informed them that the final outcome belongs to them, and that the evil turn of fate (da'ira al-su') falls upon the polytheists and the hypocrites.

It also honors the Prophet (ﷺ) for his dignity with his Lord, and promises him successive victories.

It praises the believers who supported him and pledged allegiance to him, and that Allah mentioned their likeness in the Torah (al-Tawrat) and in the Gospel (al-Injil).

[Page 143]

Then it mentions the Pledge of al-Hudaybiyya (bay'at al-Hudaybiyya) and honors those who were present at it.

It exposes those Bedouins (al-a'rab) who stayed behind from it, censures them for cowardice, greed, and bad opinion of Allah, and for lying against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It prevents them from taking part in the expedition (ghazwa) of Khaybar, and informs them that they will soon be called to another struggle (jihad). If they respond, their staying behind from al-Hudaybiyya will be forgiven.

It also promises the Prophet (ﷺ) another victory that will be followed by a greater victory, and the conquest of Makkah. Within it is a mention of a victory from Khaybar, as will come in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He has hastened for you this﴾ [al-Fath: 20].
